astronomy-0041: The discovery of which distant body prompted the International Astronomical Union to formally define a planet in 2006?
The 2005 discovery of Eris, roughly Pluto-sized, accelerated the adoption of a planet definition in 2006.
astronomy-0042: What is Pluto's largest moon called?
Charon is Pluto's largest moon, with about half Pluto's diameter, so they are sometimes considered a binary system.
astronomy-0043: Most Uranian moons are named after characters in two English writers' works. Which writer is more represented?
Uranus's moons are named after characters from Shakespeare and Alexander Pope, mostly Shakespeare.
astronomy-0044: Which gas makes up most of Venus's atmosphere?
Venus's atmosphere is about 96% carbon dioxide.
astronomy-0045: What makes up the thick clouds obscuring Venus's surface?
Venus's clouds consist mainly of sulfuric acid droplets.
astronomy-0046: Which of the Solar System's eight planets is smallest?
Mercury is the smallest of the eight planets and the closest to the Sun.
astronomy-0047: Approximately how many Earth days does Mercury take to orbit the Sun once?
Mercury's year is about 88 Earth days, the shortest planetary year.
astronomy-0048: Approximately how many Earth days are in a Martian year?
Mars orbits the Sun in about 687 Earth days.
astronomy-0049: Which planet is farthest from the Sun following Pluto's reclassification?
Neptune is the eighth and farthest planet from the Sun.
astronomy-0050: Which planet has the Solar System's coldest atmosphere despite not being farthest from the Sun?
Uranus has the coldest planetary atmosphere, with a minimum temperature of about 224 degrees below zero.
astronomy-0051: Besides frozen carbon dioxide, what is the main material in Mars's polar caps?
Mars's polar caps consist mainly of water ice covered by carbon dioxide ice.
astronomy-0052: Approximately how many days separate consecutive new crescents, defining the synodic month?
The average synodic month, from new moon to new moon, is about 29.53 days.
astronomy-0053: Approximately how many days does the Moon take to orbit Earth relative to the fixed stars?
The sidereal month is about 27.32 days, shorter than the synodic month because Earth advances in its orbit around the Sun.
astronomy-0054: Why do we always see the same face of the Moon from Earth?
The Moon does not rotate on its axis at all
Earth hides the other face with its shadow
The other face is dark and never receives sunlight
Its rotation period equals its orbital period around Earth
The Moon is tidally locked, rotating on its axis in the same time it takes to orbit Earth.
astronomy-0055: What are the dark 'seas' visible on the Moon with the naked eye?
Plains of ancient solidified basaltic lava
Lunar maria are broad dark plains formed by ancient basaltic volcanic flows.
astronomy-0056: What hypothetical body is thought to have struck ancient Earth, forming the Moon from impact debris?
The giant-impact hypothesis proposes that a Mars-sized body called Theia struck the young Earth, forming the Moon from debris.
astronomy-0057: Approximately what is the average distance between the centers of Earth and the Moon?
The Moon's average distance from Earth is about 384,400 kilometers.
astronomy-0058: Approximately how strong is lunar surface gravity compared with Earth's?
Lunar surface gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's, allowing astronauts to jump easily.
astronomy-0059: Approximately what fraction of Earth's diameter is the Moon's diameter?
The Moon's diameter is about 3474 kilometers, roughly a quarter of Earth's.
astronomy-0060: During which lunar phase can a solar eclipse occur?
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, during the new moon phase.
astronomy-0061: Why is there not a solar eclipse every lunar month?
The Moon slows its rotation each month
The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to Earth's orbital plane
The Sun moves farther from Earth each month
The Moon's roughly 5-degree orbital tilt usually makes its shadow pass north or south of Earth at new moon.
astronomy-0062: Why do the Moon and Sun appear to have roughly equal-sized disks in the sky?
The Sun is about 400 times larger and 400 times farther away
The Moon is closer to the Sun than to Earth
The Moon and Sun are the same size
The Sun's diameter is about 400 times the Moon's, and its distance about 400 times greater, making their apparent sizes roughly equal.
astronomy-0063: Approximately how long can a total solar eclipse last at most at one location on Earth?
Even under ideal conditions, totality lasts no more than about 7 and a half minutes because the Moon's shadow moves rapidly across Earth.
astronomy-0064: What astronomical cycle repeats similar solar and lunar eclipses about every 18 years and 11 days?
The Saros cycle is about 18 years and 11 days, after which the Sun, Moon, and lunar nodes return to similar positions.
astronomy-0065: Approximately how many solar years equal 235 lunar months according to the Metonic cycle?
The Metonic cycle equates 235 lunar months to approximately 19 solar years.
astronomy-0066: When the dark part of a crescent Moon appears faintly lit, where does this faint light come from?
This is earthshine: sunlight reflected from Earth faintly illuminates the Moon's dark portion.
astronomy-0067: What does 'supermoon' mean in astronomy news?
A Moon appearing red during an eclipse
A Moon seen with a total solar eclipse
A full moon occurring twice in one month
A full moon coinciding with the Moon nearing perigee
A supermoon is a full moon near its closest orbital point to Earth (perigee), making it appear slightly larger and brighter.
astronomy-0069: In which direction is the crescent marking the start of the lunar month sought?
The first crescent is seen shortly after sunset on the western horizon near the sunset position.
astronomy-0070: After sunset on which day of the lunar month does observation for the new crescent usually begin?
The crescent is sought after sunset on day twenty-nine. If seen, the new month begins; otherwise, the month is completed as thirty days.
astronomy-0071: What do astronomers call the instant when the Sun and Moon share a celestial longitude, marking the astronomical lunar month's start?
Conjunction, the astronomical new moon, is when the Moon and Sun share a celestial longitude; crescent age is counted from it.
astronomy-0072: What lunar phase shows half the disk illuminated about a week after new moon?
About a week after new moon, the Moon reaches first quarter, with half its disk illuminated.
astronomy-0073: What is the lunar phase in which more than half but less than the entire disk is illuminated called?
In the gibbous phase, more than half but less than the whole disk is illuminated.
astronomy-0074: When does a full moon usually rise?
A full moon lies opposite the Sun and rises roughly as the Sun sets.
astronomy-0075: Which lunar crater is known for bright rays extending long distances, clearly visible in the southern lunar hemisphere at full moon?
Tycho is a relatively young crater with extensive bright rays clearly visible at full moon.
astronomy-0076: Which probe took the first images of the Moon's far side in 1959?
The Soviet Luna 3 probe took the first images of the lunar far side in October 1959.
astronomy-0077: Which probe made the first soft landing on the Moon's far side in January 2019?
China's Chang'e 4 probe landed on the lunar far side on 3 January 2019, the first soft landing there.
astronomy-0079: Why does the Moon look larger near the horizon than overhead?
The atmosphere acts as a magnifying lens
It is an optical illusion in the brain's perception of size
It actually moves closer to Earth at moonrise
It reflects more sunlight near the horizon
The Moon illusion is an optical illusion; instrument measurements show no actual enlargement at the horizon.
astronomy-0080: What percentage of the Moon's surface can be seen from Earth over time thanks to lunar libration?
Libration allows us to see about 59% of the lunar surface over time rather than only 50%.
astronomy-0081: What is the largest impact crater on the Moon?
The South Pole-Aitken basin on the lunar far side is about 2240 kilometers in diameter, making it the Moon's largest crater.
astronomy-0082: How many people walked on the Moon during Apollo missions between 1969 and 1972?
Six Apollo missions landed on the Moon through 1972, and twelve astronauts walked on its surface.
astronomy-0083: In which direction is the waning crescent seen at the end of the lunar month?
The waning crescent is seen in the eastern morning sky shortly before sunrise.
astronomy-0084: What is the completely dark part of a shadow where an observer sees a total eclipse called?
The umbra is the region where the Moon blocks the Sun's entire disk.
astronomy-0085: How many days are in the lunar Hijri year?
The Hijri year consists of twelve lunar months, totaling 354 or 355 days.
astronomy-0086: After approximately how many solar years does Ramadan return to the same season?
Hijri months move through the seasons and return to their positions after about 33 solar years.
astronomy-0087: How many days are in a Hijri month?
A Hijri month has 29 or 30 days according to crescent sighting.
astronomy-0088: The Istanbul Conference criterion (1978) sets a minimum angular separation between the crescent and Sun for possible visibility. Approximately what is it?
One Istanbul Conference criterion requires the crescent's angular separation from the Sun to be at least 8 degrees.
astronomy-0090: How many lunar mansions are there in Arab astronomy?
Arabs divided the Moon's path into 28 mansions, with the Moon occupying roughly one each night.
astronomy-0091: Why did Arabs give the bright red star Aldebaran its name?
It rises after the Pleiades, as though following them
It is the first star to appear after sunset
It is the reddest star in the entire sky
Al-Dabaran means 'the follower' because it rises after the Pleiades; its scientific name became Aldebaran.
astronomy-0092: What is the Arabic name of the Pleiades star cluster, known in the West as the Seven Sisters?
Al-Thurayya is a bright open star cluster and one of the Arab lunar mansions.
astronomy-0093: What phenomenon is popularly called a 'blue moon'?
A crescent seen during the day
The Moon at its farthest point from Earth
The second full moon in one calendar month
A Moon that always turns blue after volcanic eruptions
A blue moon commonly means the second full moon in a calendar month and usually has no connection to its color.
astronomy-0094: Approximately how fast does the Moon move away from Earth each year?
The Moon recedes from Earth by about 3.8 centimeters per year due to tidal interaction.
astronomy-0095: Approximately how many eclipse seasons occur each year?
Two seasons about six months apart
New moons occur near the lunar orbital nodes in two periods about six months apart: the eclipse seasons.
astronomy-0096: What happens during a lunar eclipse?
Earth lies between the Sun and Moon, and the Moon enters Earth's shadow
The Moon moves away from the Sun and grows dimmer
The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth
A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth lies between the Sun and Moon, placing the Moon in Earth's shadow; it occurs only at full moon.
astronomy-0097: Approximately how much later does the Moon rise each successive day?
The Moon advances in its orbit each day, rising about 50 minutes later than the previous day on average.
astronomy-0098: Which space mission carried the first humans to orbit the Moon in December 1968?
Apollo 8 in December 1968 was the first crewed mission to leave Earth orbit and orbit the Moon.
astronomy-0099: Where did Apollo 11's lunar module land in July 1969?
The Eagle module landed in the Sea of Tranquility (Mare Tranquillitatis) on 20 July 1969.
astronomy-0100: What lunar module landed Apollo 11's two astronauts on the Moon in 1969?
The lunar module was Eagle, while the command module was Columbia.
astronomy-0101: Approximately what percentage of the Solar System's total mass is in the Sun?
The Sun contains about 99.86% of the Solar System's mass and is about 330 thousand times Earth's mass.
astronomy-0102: Approximately how many years ago did the Sun form, according to scientists' estimates?
The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago when part of a molecular cloud collapsed under gravity.
astronomy-0103: To which spectral class does the Sun belong?
An extremely hot class A white dwarf
An extremely hot class O blue giant
The Sun is classified as G2V: a class G star in the main-sequence phase.
astronomy-0104: What produces the enormous energy radiated by the Sun?
Gases burning with oxygen in its outer layers
Hydrogen nuclei fusing into helium in its core
Its continuous slow contraction under its own gravity
Uranium and thorium nuclei splitting inside it
The Sun produces energy through nuclear fusion, converting hydrogen into helium in its core.
astronomy-0105: What is the Sun's expected fate after its core hydrogen runs out billions of years from now?
It gradually cools into a gas planet
It immediately contracts into a neutron star
It expands into a red giant and ultimately becomes a white dwarf
It explodes as a supernova and becomes a black hole
The Sun lacks enough mass for a supernova; it will expand into a red giant and end as a white dwarf.
astronomy-0106: What is the visible solar layer that emits most of its visible light called?
The photosphere is the layer from which a star's light emerges, appearing as the Sun's surface.
astronomy-0107: Why do sunspots look dark on the Sun's disk?
They are cooler than surrounding areas
They are shadows of planets passing before the Sun
They are dust clouds blocking light
They are holes admitting the light of dark space
Sunspots are cooler regions (about 3000-4500 kelvin) due to concentrated magnetic fields, so they appear relatively dark.
astronomy-0108: Approximately how many years is the average solar cycle during which sunspot numbers change?
The average solar cycle (Schwabe cycle) lasts about 11 years, with sunspot numbers increasing and then decreasing.
astronomy-0109: What causes auroras near the poles?
Sunlight reflecting from extensive polar ice in winter
Small meteors burning in the upper atmosphere at night
The solar wind's effect on Earth's magnetosphere
Auroras arise when solar wind disturbs Earth's magnetosphere and charged particles collide with the atmosphere.
astronomy-0110: Its poles rotate much faster than its equator
It does not rotate on its axis at all
Its equator rotates faster than regions near its poles
It completes a rotation in exactly 24 hours
The Sun is not solid: its equator rotates in about 25.7 days, with longer periods toward the poles.
astronomy-0111: What type of object is Sirius's faint companion, Sirius B?
Sirius is a binary system: a main-sequence star accompanied by a faint white dwarf called Sirius B.
astronomy-0112: What is the Arabic name for Canopus, the second-brightest star in the night sky?
Canopus was known in Arab astronomy as Suhayl; it is the second-brightest star after Sirius.
astronomy-0113: What is the brightest star in the entire night sky?
Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, with an apparent magnitude of -1.46.
astronomy-0114: What is the brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere?
Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere and the fourth-brightest star in the sky.
astronomy-0115: Why is Polaris used to find north?
It is so close to the north celestial pole that it barely moves
It is the brightest star of all in every season
It appears day and night everywhere on Earth
It always rises in the north and sets in the south
Polaris is less than one degree from the north celestial pole, remaining nearly stationary above north.
astronomy-0116: Polaris is Ursa Minor's brightest star, at the tip of its tail.
astronomy-0117: Which two Big Dipper stars in Ursa Major point toward Polaris along the line joining them?
Extending a line from Merak through Dubhe leads to Polaris.
astronomy-0118: What type of star is Betelgeuse in Orion?
Betelgeuse is a red supergiant, among the largest stars visible to the naked eye.
astronomy-0119: From which Arabic phrase is the name Betelgeuse derived?
The name derives from the Arabic phrase Yad al-Jawza, later distorted in Latin transmission.
astronomy-0121: What collective name is given to the three aligned stars Alnitak, Alnilam, and Mintaka?
Alnitak, Alnilam, and Mintaka are three aligned stars forming Orion's Belt.
astronomy-0122: From which Arabic phrase is the name Altair derived?
Altair is a shortened form of the Arabic phrase Al-Nasr al-Ta'ir.
astronomy-0123: What is the Arabic name of Vega, one of the brightest stars in the northern sky?
Vega comes from Waqi in the Arabic phrase Al-Nasr al-Waqi.
astronomy-0124: Because of Earth's axial precession, which bright star will become the north pole star in about 12 thousand years?
Earth's axis slowly changes direction, making Vega a northern pole star around 13724 CE.
astronomy-0125: Approximately how long is a full cycle of Earth's axial precession?
Earth's axis traces a cone in the sky over about 26 thousand years, a cycle called precession.
astronomy-0127: Which three stars form the Summer Triangle in the northern sky?
The Summer Triangle consists of three bright stars: Vega, Altair, and Deneb.
astronomy-0129: Why does Algol dim regularly about every three days?
A companion star passes in front of it, partially eclipsing it
It pulsates, expanding and contracting regularly every three days
A dense dust cloud orbits and obscures it
Algol is an eclipsing binary: the dimmer star passes before the brighter one every 2.86 days, reducing its light.
astronomy-0131: What is the Arabic name of Capella, the brightest star in Auriga?
Capella was known to Arabs as Al-Ayyuq.
astronomy-0132: What is the largest known globular star cluster in the Milky Way?
Omega Centauri is the largest and most massive known globular cluster in our galaxy.
astronomy-0133: Which of the 88 constellations covers the largest area of sky?
Hydra is the largest modern constellation by area and the longest.
astronomy-0134: What is the smallest modern constellation by area?
Crux, the Southern Cross, is the smallest of the 88 constellations by area, although among the easiest to recognize.
astronomy-0135: How many constellations does the International Astronomical Union officially recognize to divide the sky?
The International Astronomical Union adopted a list of 88 constellations in 1922 and defined their boundaries in 1928.
astronomy-0136: What is the most common type of star in the Milky Way?
Red dwarfs are by far the most common fusion-burning stars in our galaxy, but are too faint to see with the naked eye.
astronomy-0137: What mainly causes stars to twinkle when viewed from Earth's surface?
Their light passes through turbulent atmospheric layers
Earth's orbital motion around the Sun
The stars themselves change brightness several times a second
Stars rotate extremely quickly on their axes in space
Stars twinkle because their light passes through turbulent air layers of changing density, continually deflecting it slightly.
astronomy-0138: Which bright nebula is visible to the naked eye below Orion's Belt?
The Orion Nebula (M42) is among the brightest nebulae and can be seen with the naked eye even from light-polluted areas.
astronomy-0139: Which letter denotes the hottest stars in the spectral classification O B A F G K M?
The classification begins with the hottest class O and ends with the coolest class M.
astronomy-0140: What does the famous Hertzsprung-Russell diagram represent?
The relationship between stellar luminosity and spectral class or temperature
Planetary orbits around the Sun and speeds at each point
The distribution of galaxies by distance and recession speed
Lunar phases and the illuminated fraction of the disk each night
The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram plots stars by luminosity and spectral class or temperature.
astronomy-0141: Which researcher detected the first pulsar signals in 1967?
Jocelyn Bell detected the first pulsar signals in August 1967 using a radio telescope she helped build.
astronomy-0142: Approximately what is the Chandrasekhar limit, the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf?
The Chandrasekhar limit is about 1.4 solar masses; above it, electron pressure cannot resist gravity.
astronomy-0143: Approximately how many light-years equal one parsec?
A parsec is a distance unit equal to about 3.26 light-years or about 206 thousand astronomical units.
astronomy-0144: In the apparent magnitude scale, what does a smaller star magnitude number mean?
The star looks brighter to us
The star is farther away in space
The star has a cooler surface
The star is smaller than others
The magnitude scale is reversed: smaller numbers mean brighter objects, so Sirius has a negative magnitude.
astronomy-0145: The distance light travels through a vacuum in one year
The time sunlight takes to reach the farthest planet
The time Earth takes to orbit the Sun once
The distance between the Sun and the galactic center
A light-year is a distance unit, not time, equal to about 9.46 trillion kilometers.
astronomy-0146: What usually remains of a massive star's core after a supernova explosion?
A white dwarf or brown dwarf
A giant gas planet orbiting the core
A neutron star or black hole
After a massive star explodes as a supernova, its core collapses into a neutron star or black hole depending on mass.
astronomy-0147: What is a rotating neutron star that emits regular radiation beams called?
A pulsar is a rapidly rotating neutron star whose radiation beams reach us as regular pulses.
astronomy-0148: What is a huge cloud of gas and dust where stars are born called?
Nebulae are interstellar clouds of gas and dust, many of which form new stars.
astronomy-0149: What was the first human-made satellite launched into Earth orbit on 4 October 1957?
The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957, making it history's first artificial satellite.
astronomy-0150: What was the name of the dog that became the first animal to orbit Earth aboard Sputnik 2 in November 1957?
Sputnik 2 carried Laika on 3 November 1957, the first animal to orbit Earth.
astronomy-0151: Which spacecraft carried Yuri Gagarin on the first human spaceflight on 12 April 1961?
Gagarin flew aboard Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961, completing one Earth orbit.
astronomy-0152: Approximately how long was Yuri Gagarin's flight around Earth on 12 April 1961?
Vostok 1's flight lasted about 108 minutes from launch to landing.
astronomy-0153: Who was the first woman to travel into space, in June 1963?
Valentina Tereshkova flew aboard Vostok 6 on 16 June 1963, becoming the first woman in space.
astronomy-0154: Who first left his spacecraft to perform a spacewalk on 18 March 1965?
Alexei Leonov exited Voskhod 2 on 18 March 1965 for the first spacewalk.
astronomy-0155: Which capsule carried John Glenn around Earth in 1962, making him the first American to orbit it?
John Glenn orbited Earth three times aboard Friendship 7 on 20 February 1962.
astronomy-0156: On what date did Apollo 11's lunar module land on the Moon?
Apollo 11 launched on 16 July 1969, its lunar module landed on 20 July, and it returned to Earth on 24 July.
astronomy-0157: Which astronaut stepped onto the Moon after Neil Armstrong during Apollo 11?
Buzz Aldrin stepped down about 19 minutes after Armstrong, while Collins remained in orbit.
astronomy-0158: Which Apollo 11 astronaut remained in the command module orbiting the Moon without landing?
Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit in Columbia while Armstrong and Aldrin descended to the surface.
astronomy-0159: What happened to Apollo 13 in April 1970?
It went off course and orbited Mars
An oxygen tank exploded, canceling the landing, and the crew returned safely
It landed at an unplanned lunar site
The spacecraft burned on the launch pad
An oxygen tank exploded in the service module, canceling the lunar landing; the three astronauts returned safely.
astronomy-0160: What was the last Apollo mission to land on the Moon, in December 1972?
Apollo 17 in December 1972 was the last Apollo mission and the last human lunar landing of the twentieth century.
astronomy-0161: What giant rocket launched crewed Apollo missions to the Moon between 1968 and 1972?
The Saturn V rocket carried the Apollo missions to the Moon.
astronomy-0162: On which mission was the lunar rover first used on the Moon in 1971?
The lunar rover was first used on Apollo 15 in 1971.
astronomy-0163: Which probe made the first soft lunar landing in February 1966?
The Soviet Luna 9 probe soft-landed on the Moon on 3 February 1966 and sent surface photographs.
astronomy-0164: Which probe sent the first close-up images of Mars during its July 1965 flyby?
Mariner 4 flew past Mars in July 1965, sending the first close-up images of another planet.
astronomy-0165: Which American spacecraft landed on Mars in July 1976 and sent surface images?
Viking 1 landed on Mars on 20 July 1976 and operated on its surface for years.
astronomy-0166: What was the first rover to move on Mars, as part of the 1997 Pathfinder mission?
Sojourner, carried by Mars Pathfinder in 1997, was the first rover on Mars.
astronomy-0167: In which Martian crater did Curiosity land in August 2012?
Curiosity landed in Gale crater on 6 August 2012.
astronomy-0168: What small helicopter accompanied Perseverance to Mars and first flew there in April 2021?
Ingenuity flew on 19 April 2021, becoming the first aircraft to make a powered flight on another planet.
astronomy-0169: In which month and year did the UAE's Hope probe enter Mars orbit?
Hope launched in July 2020 and entered Mars orbit on 9 February 2021.
astronomy-0170: From which country was the UAE's Hope probe launched toward Mars in July 2020?
Hope launched on a Japanese rocket from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan.
astronomy-0171: Aboard which space shuttle did Prince Sultan bin Salman travel in 1985, becoming the first Arab in space?
Prince Sultan bin Salman participated in Discovery mission STS-51-G in June 1985.
astronomy-0172: Who was the first Syrian astronaut, traveling to the Mir space station in July 1987?
Muhammed Faris traveled to Mir in 1987, becoming the first Syrian and second Arab in space.
astronomy-0173: Who was the first Emirati astronaut, visiting the International Space Station in September 2019?
Hazza Al Mansouri launched toward the International Space Station on 25 September 2019.
astronomy-0174: Who was the first Arab astronaut to perform a spacewalk outside the International Space Station, in April 2023?
Sultan Al Neyadi performed the first Arab spacewalk on 28 April 2023 during his long mission on the International Space Station.
astronomy-0175: Who was the first Saudi woman to travel into space, in May 2023?
Rayyanah Barnawi launched to the International Space Station on the Axiom 2 mission in May 2023.
astronomy-0177: What defect was discovered in Hubble after its 1990 launch and repaired during a 1993 servicing mission?
Fuel leaking from its main engines
A flaw in its primary mirror's shape blurred images
Complete failure of its solar panels
Its orbit drifting toward the atmosphere
Hubble's primary mirror was polished to an inaccurate shape, causing spherical aberration corrected by a servicing mission in December 1993.
astronomy-0178: On what date was the James Webb Space Telescope launched?
James Webb launched on 25 December 2021 aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana.
astronomy-0179: In which radiation range does James Webb primarily observe the universe?
James Webb was designed to observe infrared radiation to see extremely distant galaxies and dust-obscured objects.
astronomy-0180: Where has James Webb been located since reaching its destination in January 2022?
Near the second Lagrange point L2, about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth
On the Moon's south polar surface
In low Earth orbit near the International Space Station
James Webb orbits the Sun near Lagrange point L2, about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
astronomy-0181: Which spacecraft became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space, in August 2012?
Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause on 25 August 2012, becoming the first spacecraft to reach interstellar space.
astronomy-0182: What famous photograph taken by Voyager 1 in 1990 shows Earth as a tiny dot from far away?
Voyager 1 took Pale Blue Dot on 14 February 1990 from about 6 billion kilometers away.
astronomy-0183: Which spacecraft flew past Pluto on 14 July 2015, taking its first detailed images?
New Horizons flew past Pluto on 14 July 2015, revealing its terrain for the first time.
astronomy-0184: How did Cassini end its Saturn mission in September 2017?
By deliberately plunging into Saturn's atmosphere
By returning to Earth with samples
By heading outside the Solar System
Controllers directed Cassini into Saturn's atmosphere on 15 September 2017 to avoid contaminating potentially habitable moons.
astronomy-0185: What probe landed on Titan, Saturn's largest moon, in January 2005?
Huygens separated from Cassini and landed on Titan on 14 January 2005, the most distant landing in the Solar System.
astronomy-0186: Which craft made the first landing on a comet's nucleus in November 2014?
Philae, carried by Rosetta, landed on comet 67P on 12 November 2014.
astronomy-0187: Which spacecraft entered Jupiter orbit in July 2016 to study its interior and magnetic field?
Juno entered Jupiter orbit on 4 July 2016.
astronomy-0188: Which spacecraft launched in August 2018 to approach the Sun more closely than any previous craft?
Parker Solar Probe launched on 12 August 2018 to study the solar corona at close range.
astronomy-0189: Since what year has the International Space Station been continuously inhabited?
The first resident crew reached the station on 2 November 2000, and it has been continuously occupied since.
astronomy-0190: Which Soviet and later Russian space station launched its first module in 1986 and was deorbited in 2001?
Mir's core module launched in 1986, and the station underwent a controlled deorbit in March 2001.
astronomy-0191: What was the first American space station, launched in 1973?
Skylab launched on 14 May 1973 as the United States' first space station.
astronomy-0192: Which space shuttle made the shuttle program's first flight in April 1981?
Columbia launched on STS-1 on 12 April 1981, the first orbital shuttle flight.
astronomy-0193: Which country's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023?
India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023.
astronomy-0194: What scientific discovery was associated with the first American satellite, Explorer 1, in 1958?
Explorer 1 recorded readings in 1958 that led to the discovery of the Van Allen radiation belts.
astronomy-0195: What Chinese rover landed on Mars in May 2021?
Zhurong landed on Mars in May 2021 as part of the Tianwen-1 mission.
astronomy-0196: Which spacecraft first crossed the asteroid belt and flew past Jupiter, in 1973?
Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and fly past Jupiter, in December 1973.
astronomy-0197: Which Soviet probe made the first landing on another planet while transmitting surface data, in December 1970?
Venera 7 landed on Venus on 15 December 1970 and transmitted surface data, the first successful landing on another planet.
astronomy-0198: From which asteroid did OSIRIS-REx return samples to Earth in September 2023?
OSIRIS-REx returned a capsule containing Bennu samples to Earth on 24 September 2023.
astronomy-0199: From which asteroid did Japan's Hayabusa return samples to Earth in 2010?
Hayabusa returned to Earth in June 2010 with Itokawa samples, the first samples returned from an asteroid.
astronomy-0200: What type of galaxy is our Milky Way?
The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy about 87 thousand light-years across.
astronomy-0201: Approximately how many stars does the Milky Way contain according to scientific estimates?
The Milky Way's stars are estimated at between 100 and 400 billion.
astronomy-0202: Approximately how far is the Solar System from the Milky Way's center?
The Solar System lies about 27 thousand light-years from the galactic center, on the inner edge of the Orion Arm.
astronomy-0203: Approximately how many million years does the Solar System take to orbit the galactic center once?
This period is called a galactic year and is estimated at about 225 to 250 million years.
astronomy-0204: Approximately how far is the Andromeda Galaxy from Earth?
Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away, the nearest large spiral galaxy to us.
astronomy-0206: Which two dwarf irregular galaxies appear as faint clouds in the southern sky?
Ursa Minor and Draco dwarf galaxies
The Magellanic Clouds are two dwarf irregular galaxies in the southern celestial hemisphere.
astronomy-0207: When was the first black hole image, showing the supermassive black hole in M87, published?
The Event Horizon Telescope team published the first black hole image on 10 April 2019, based on observations from 2017.
astronomy-0208: What is the event horizon around a black hole?
The point where time stops only for a distant observer
The ring of glowing gas orbiting it
The boundary from within which nothing, even light, escapes
The farthest reach of its gravity
The event horizon is the boundary from inside which nothing can escape, not even light.
astronomy-0209: When were gravitational waves first directly detected?
LIGO detected the first gravitational waves on 14 September 2015, announcing this in February 2016.
astronomy-0210: What is the estimated age of the universe based on Planck satellite data and modern models?
Modern models with Planck data estimate the universe's age at about 13.8 billion years.
astronomy-0211: Which astronomer published the relationship between galaxy distance and recession speed in 1929, indicating cosmic expansion?
Hubble's law was attributed to Edwin Hubble's research published in 1929.
astronomy-0212: What does redshift in a distant galaxy's light spectrum indicate?
It is a newly formed galaxy
It is moving away from us
It is hotter than our galaxy
When a light source recedes from an observer, its spectrum shifts toward red; when approaching, it shifts toward blue.
astronomy-0213: Which two scientists accidentally discovered the cosmic microwave background in 1964?
Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered the cosmic microwave background in 1964 using a radio receiver at Bell Labs.
astronomy-0214: Which American astronomer's study of galaxy rotation curves helped establish the concept of dark matter?
Vera Rubin showed that galaxy edges rotate faster than expected, providing major evidence for dark matter.
astronomy-0215: An extremely luminous active galactic nucleus
A gas cloud where stars form
A comet arriving from outside the Solar System
A quasar is an extremely luminous active galactic nucleus powered by a supermassive black hole consuming surrounding material.
astronomy-0216: Which astronomer discovered the relationship between Cepheid variability periods and true luminosity, enabling galaxy distance measurements?
Henrietta Leavitt discovered the Cepheid period-luminosity relationship, enabling cosmic distance measurements.
astronomy-0217: Which scientist is credited with coining 'Big Bang' on a radio program despite opposing the theory?
Fred Hoyle is credited with coining 'Big Bang' on BBC radio and opposed the theory.
astronomy-0218: When is Halley's Comet expected to return to the inner Solar System after its 1986 appearance?
Halley's Comet last appeared in 1986, with its next return expected in mid-2061.
astronomy-0219: On what observation did Edmond Halley base his prediction of the return of the comet named after him?
The 1531, 1607, and 1682 comets had similar orbits, indicating one returning comet
The comet always appears in the same calendar month
Its tail grows longer with each appearance, indicating its imminent return
It follows Jupiter's orbit and returns when Jupiter returns to its position
Halley noted similar orbital elements for the comets of 1531, 1607, and 1682, concluding they were one comet returning about every 76 years.
astronomy-0220: In which direction does a comet's ion tail point?
In the comet's direction of motion
Solar radiation pressure and solar wind push tail material, making it point away from the Sun.
astronomy-0221: What famous description was applied to a comet's nucleus in Fred Whipple's model?
Comet nuclei were described as dirty snowballs because they mix ice, dust, and rock.
astronomy-0222: Which comet supplies the debris causing the summer Perseid meteor shower?
The Perseids are associated with Swift-Tuttle's debris, which Earth crosses each summer.
astronomy-0223: Approximately how long ago did the asteroid that created Mexico's Chicxulub crater strike?
Chicxulub crater formed slightly over 66 million years ago when an asteroid about 10 kilometers across struck.
astronomy-0224: In what year did the Tunguska event flatten millions of Siberian trees when a space object exploded in the atmosphere?
The Tunguska explosion occurred over central Siberia on 30 June 1908.
astronomy-0225: Over which region did a large meteor explode on 15 February 2013, breaking windows in thousands of buildings?
The Chelyabinsk meteor exploded over Russia's southern Urals on 15 February 2013.
astronomy-0226: Which planet was struck by fragments of Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 in July 1994?
Shoemaker-Levy 9 broke apart and its fragments struck Jupiter in July 1994, the first directly observed collision between two extraterrestrial Solar System bodies.
astronomy-0227: For how many months was Comet Hale-Bopp visible to the naked eye in the 1990s, setting a record?
Thanks to its enormous nucleus, Hale-Bopp remained visible to the naked eye for a record 18 months.
astronomy-0228: It was a second natural moon that had long orbited Earth
It was a periodic comet returning near the Sun about every ten years
It was the largest known asteroid in the belt between Mars and Jupiter
It was the first confirmed object crossing the Solar System from outside it
'Oumuamua was the first confirmed interstellar object observed crossing the Solar System.
astronomy-0230: When did Isaac Newton complete the first known working reflecting telescope?
Newton completed his first reflecting telescope in 1668, the earliest known working reflecting telescope.
astronomy-0231: What collects light and forms the image in a reflecting telescope?
Reflecting telescopes use curved mirrors to reflect light and form images, unlike refracting telescopes, which use lenses.
astronomy-0232: What is the dish diameter of China's FAST radio telescope, built in a natural mountain depression?
FAST's dish is 500 meters across and was built in a natural depression in Guizhou.
astronomy-0233: Which chemical element was first detected in sunlight's spectrum during an 1868 eclipse before being found on Earth?
An unknown yellow spectral line was observed in sunlight in 1868 and attributed to a new element named helium after the Sun.
astronomy-0235: In what year was the first planet orbiting a Sunlike star, 51 Pegasi b, announced?
Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced the discovery of 51 Pegasi b on 6 October 1995.
astronomy-0236: What main method did the Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, use to discover thousands of exoplanets?
Detecting a star's dimming when a planet passes in front
Directly imaging planets by light reflected from their surfaces
Detecting radio signals from distant planets
Kepler used the transit method: detecting the slight drop in starlight when a planet passes in front.
astronomy-0238: What is a star's habitable zone?
The region free of asteroids, comets, and collision debris
The range of orbits where water could remain liquid on a planet's surface
The region reached by visible starlight without harmful radiation
The region directly between the star and its nearest planet
The habitable zone is the range of orbits with temperatures allowing liquid water on the surface of a planet with a sufficient atmosphere.
astronomy-0239: What is the supermassive black hole at the Milky Way's center called?
At the galactic center is Sagittarius A*, a strong radio source and a supermassive black hole of about 4 million solar masses.
astronomy-0240: Which celestial object did Edwin Hubble confirm around 1924 as a separate galaxy outside the Milky Way by measuring its distance?
Hubble observed Cepheid stars in the Andromeda 'Nebula,' proving it was very distant and a separate galaxy.
astronomy-0241: How were Uranus's rings discovered in March 1977?
By directly imaging them with Hubble
By measuring their gravity with an orbiting probe
By observing a distant star dim repeatedly before and after being hidden by the planet
Astronomers observing a star's occultation by Uranus noticed five brief disappearances before and after the occultation, revealing rings.
astronomy-0242: What is thought to make up most of the universe's matter mass despite being invisible and emitting no light?
Evidence suggests dark matter constitutes about 85% of the universe's matter mass and does not interact with light.
astronomy-0244: What type of object is a brown dwarf?
A rocky planet covered in deserts and brown dust
A dead star that has completely cooled after being a bright white dwarf
A large dark carbon-rich asteroid in the asteroid belt
An object larger than a planet but too small to sustain hydrogen fusion
A brown dwarf has a mass between the largest gas planets and smallest stars, insufficient to sustain ordinary hydrogen fusion.
astronomy-0245: Which nebula is the remnant of the supernova recorded by Chinese, Arab, and Japanese astronomers in 1054 CE?
The Crab Nebula is the remnant of supernova SN 1054 observed by Chinese, Arab, and Japanese astronomers.
astronomy-0246: Why are major astronomical observatories often built on high mountaintops in dry regions?
High temperatures there improve mirrors and lenses
Less air, moisture, and turbulence above them, and distance from city lights
Weaker gravity stabilizes telescopes and makes them easy to move
Stars are actually closer, appearing larger and clearer
Altitude and dryness reduce atmospheric and moisture effects, while distance from cities reduces light pollution, improving observations.
astronomy-0247: Which model did Ptolemy establish in Al-Majisti (Almagest), remaining accepted for over twelve hundred years?
Al-Majisti established the geocentric model, which remained accepted for over 1200 years.
astronomy-0248: Which Greek astronomer proposed the first known Sun-centered model in the third century BCE?
Aristarchus of Samos proposed the first known heliocentric model, in which Earth orbits the Sun.
astronomy-0249: What is the Greek scholar Eratosthenes remembered for in the history of astronomy and geography?
Discovering the precession of the equinoxes
Eratosthenes is known for the first known calculation of Earth's circumference using differences in solar shadows between two cities.
astronomy-0250: According to Kepler's first law, what shape is a planet's orbit around the Sun?
A perfect circle with the Sun at its center
An ellipse with the Sun at one focus
A spiral gradually tightening around the Sun
An open parabola with the Sun at its vertex
Kepler's first law states that a planet's orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.
astronomy-0251: According to Kepler's second law, when does a planet move fastest in its orbit?
At a constant speed throughout its orbit
At its farthest point from the Sun
At its closest point to the Sun
The line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times, so the planet speeds up as it approaches the Sun.
astronomy-0252: What does Kepler's third law of planetary motion relate?
A planet's mass to the cube of its diameter and square of its average density
The square of a planet's orbital period to the cube of its orbital semimajor axis
A planet's surface temperature to the square of its mean solar distance
A planet's rotation speed to the number and mass of its moons
The third law states that the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the orbit's semimajor axis.
astronomy-0253: What did Galileo observe on Venus with his telescope in 1610 that supported planets orbiting the Sun?
Moving dark spots on its surface
Galileo observed Venus's full set of phases, inconsistent with Ptolemy's model but consistent with Venus orbiting the Sun.
astronomy-0254: What booklet published Galileo's first telescopic observations in March 1610?
Hiwar Hawla al-Nizamayn al-Ra'isayn (Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief Systems)
Galileo published Al-Rasul al-Najmi (Sidereus Nuncius) on 13 March 1610, describing Jupiter's moons and lunar mountains.
astronomy-0255: In what year was Newton's Al-Mabadi al-Riyadiyya lil-Falsafa al-Tabi'iyya (Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), formulating universal gravitation, published?
The first edition of Al-Mabadi (Principia) was published in 1687.
astronomy-0256: How did Danish astronomer Ole Romer show in 1676 that light has a finite speed?
By observing delays in eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io
By measuring sound speed in air and comparing it with light speed
By observing distant starlight bending near the Sun
By timing light reflected from a distant mountaintop mirror
Romer noticed that Io's eclipses occurred later as Earth moved away from Jupiter, concluding that light takes time to travel.
astronomy-0257: Which Muslim astronomer recorded the earliest known observation of Andromeda in 964 CE, describing it as a 'small cloud'?
In Kitab Suwar al-Kawakib al-Thabita in 964 CE, Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi described Andromeda as a small cloud.
astronomy-0258: Which Muslim astronomer calculated the solar year as 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes, and 24 seconds?
Al-Battani's solar year calculation differed from today's accepted value by only two minutes and 22 seconds.
astronomy-0259: In which city did Ulugh Beg build his famous observatory in the 1420s?
Ulugh Beg built his observatory in Samarkand, now Uzbekistan, in the 1420s.
astronomy-0260: Which fourteenth-century Damascene astronomer devised a lunar-motion model very similar to Copernicus's later model?
Ibn al-Shatir's lunar model was later found to closely resemble Copernicus's.
astronomy-0261: What was an astronomical book containing tables for calculating Sun, Moon, and planet positions called in Islamic civilization?
A zij is an astronomical book containing tables for calculating celestial positions.
astronomy-0262: Which Greek astronomer is known for discovering the precession of the equinoxes in the second century BCE?
Hipparchus discovered the precession of the equinoxes and is also considered the founder of trigonometry.
astronomy-0263: Which radiation type did William Herschel discover in experiments with sunlight?
William Herschel discovered infrared radiation by measuring temperatures across the solar spectrum and beyond red.
astronomy-0264: Which Dutch astronomer discovered Titan, Saturn's largest moon, and studied its rings?
Christiaan Huygens discovered Titan in 1655 and explained Saturn's ring structure.
astronomy-0265: Which astronomical event was used in 1919 to test Einstein's prediction of starlight bending near the Sun?
During the 29 May 1919 eclipse, Eddington and Dyson measured star positions near the Sun's disk and found the predicted deflection.
astronomy-0266: Which American astronomer's stellar cataloging helped develop the modern spectral classification system?
Annie Jump Cannon cataloged hundreds of thousands of stars, contributing fundamentally to today's spectral classification.
astronomy-0267: What did Cecilia Payne establish about stellar composition in her 1925 doctoral thesis?
Stars have the same composition as Earth's crust
Stars consist mainly of hydrogen and helium
Stars are hot solid bodies surrounded by glowing gases
Stars consist mainly of molten iron and nickel
Cecilia Payne showed in 1925 that stars consist mainly of hydrogen and helium.
astronomy-0268: Why did Charles Messier compile his famous eighteenth-century catalog of nebulae and clusters?
To locate bright stars for ocean navigators
To avoid confusing these objects with the comets he sought
To count the brightest stars and rank their magnitudes
To map the entire Milky Way and its spiral arms
Messier hunted comets and cataloged stationary fuzzy objects resembling comets to avoid mistaking them.
astronomy-0269: Which engineer announced radio waves from the Milky Way in 1933, pioneering radio astronomy?
Karl Jansky announced the discovery of radio waves from the Milky Way in April 1933.
astronomy-0271: What is the summer solstice in a hemisphere?
The day Earth is closest to the Sun
The day the Sun disappears from the pole
The year's longest day and shortest night
The first day with equal day and night in that hemisphere
The summer solstice has the longest daylight period and shortest night of the year in that hemisphere.
astronomy-0272: A red glow remaining on the northern horizon all winter night
The Sun remaining above the horizon all day in polar summer
Sunlight reflected by high clouds hours after sunset
The Sun and Moon appearing overhead together at midnight
In summer, north of the Arctic Circle and south of the Antarctic Circle, the Sun remains visible throughout the day.
astronomy-0273: Approximately what is Earth's escape velocity at its surface?
Escape velocity from Earth's surface is about 11.19 kilometers per second.
astronomy-0274: Approximately how high above the equator is geostationary orbit?
Geostationary orbit lies about 35,786 kilometers above the equator.
astronomy-0275: How many Lagrange points exist in a two-body orbital system such as Earth and the Sun?
A two-body system has five Lagrange points, L1 through L5, all in the orbital plane.
astronomy-0276: What is the point on the celestial sphere directly above an observer's head called?
The zenith is directly above the observer, opposite the nadir beneath their feet.
astronomy-0277: Which celestial coordinate corresponds to geographic latitude?
Declination corresponds to geographic latitude projected onto the celestial sphere; right ascension corresponds to longitude.
astronomy-0278: Approximately how long is Earth's sidereal day, its rotation period relative to distant stars?
A sidereal day is about 23 hours, 56 minutes, and 4 seconds, roughly 4 minutes shorter than a solar day.
astronomy-0279: Why is a day added to February about every four years in the Gregorian calendar?
A lunar month falls one day behind a calendar month every four years
February is shorter than other months, so its deficit is periodically compensated
The solar year exceeds 365 days by about a quarter-day
Earth's rotation slows every four years
The average tropical year is about 365.2422 days, so the extra quarter-day accumulates to roughly one day every four years.
astronomy-0280: When is an outer planet such as Mars said to be in opposition relative to Earth?
When it is directly behind the Sun and invisible from Earth
When it is closest to the Sun in its orbit
When it is opposite the Sun in Earth's sky
When its distances from the Sun and Earth are exactly equal
Opposition occurs when an object lies opposite the Sun on the celestial sphere as seen from Earth.
astronomy-0281: What is the Bortle scale used by amateur astronomers?
A nine-level scale of night-sky darkness
A scale for lunar tremor intensity
A scale for solar wind speed near Earth's orbit
A scale for planetary impact crater sizes
The Bortle scale has nine levels measuring night-sky brightness at a location.
astronomy-0282: How many degrees below the horizon is the Sun when astronomical twilight ends and full night begins?
When the Sun reaches 18 degrees below the horizon, sky illumination is nearly absent and night begins.
astronomy-0283: What causes the green flash sometimes seen at sunset over a clear horizon?
The green sea reflecting on the Sun's edge
Bright Venus appearing beside the Sun's edge
Different atmospheric refraction of light's colors
Solar coronal gases glowing near the horizon
The atmosphere separates sunlight's colors through wavelength-dependent refraction, briefly showing green at the edge.
astronomy-0284: At what altitude does the International Aeronautical Federation conventionally place the Karman line between the atmosphere and space?
The International Aeronautical Federation defines the Karman line at 100 kilometers above sea level.
astronomy-0285: Why do astronauts float inside the International Space Station?
The station contains a special gas much lighter than air
Lunar gravity balances Earth's gravity there
They and the station are in continuous free fall around Earth
Earth's gravity completely vanishes at that altitude
Gravity at station altitude is close to surface gravity, but the station and astronauts fall freely together around Earth, producing weightlessness.
astronomy-0286: Sunlight reflected from planets and moons toward Earth
Huge gas vortices on the visible solar surface
Hot air currents blowing toward Earth from the Sun in summer
A stream of charged particles emitted from the solar corona
The solar wind is a stream of charged particles released from the Sun's corona.
astronomy-0287: Why does Mars sometimes appear to move backward among the stars in Earth's sky?
Jupiter's gravity pulls it backward when nearby
Earth overtakes it in its faster inner orbit
It actually reverses its orbit around the Sun for several months
Retrograde motion is apparent: faster-orbiting Earth overtakes Mars, making it seem to move backward.
astronomy-0288: On which moon is Verona Rupes, possibly the Solar System's tallest cliff?
Verona Rupes is a cliff on Uranus's moon Miranda, about 20 kilometers high and possibly the Solar System's tallest.
astronomy-0289: What distinguishes the surface of Saturn's moon Mimas?
The enormous Herschel crater relative to the moon's size
Mimas has Herschel crater, one of the Solar System's largest craters relative to its host body's size.
astronomy-0290: What striking surface color feature does Saturn's moon Iapetus have?
Its color changes between blue and green daily
Its leading hemisphere is very dark and the other bright
It is transparent, showing stars through it
It is deep red like Mars
Iapetus has a striking contrast between its dark leading hemisphere and bright trailing hemisphere.
astronomy-0291: Which Jovian moon has one of the Solar System's oldest and most heavily cratered surfaces?
Callisto's surface is among the oldest and most cratered in the Solar System, almost entirely covered in impact craters.
astronomy-0292: What is the only known Solar System moon with its own internally generated magnetic field?
Ganymede is the only natural moon known to have an internally generated magnetic field.
astronomy-0293: Which planetary moon orbits closest to its planet's surface, at an altitude of only about six thousand kilometers?
Phobos orbits about 6000 kilometers above Mars's surface, making it the closest natural moon to its planet.
astronomy-0294: Approximately how many times greater is atmospheric pressure on Venus's surface than on Earth's?
Pressure on Venus's surface is about 92 times Earth's sea-level pressure.
astronomy-0295: On which planet is the large Caloris impact basin, about 1550 kilometers in diameter?
Caloris Planitia is a plain within a large impact basin on Mercury about 1550 kilometers across.
astronomy-0296: Which probe discovered Jupiter's faint rings in 1979?
Voyager 1 discovered Jupiter's main ring in 1979.
astronomy-0297: What geometric shape do clouds around Saturn's north pole form?
An approximately hexagonal persistent cloud pattern surrounds Saturn's north pole.
astronomy-0298: On which planet did Voyager 2 observe the Great Dark Spot in 1989?
The Great Dark Spot was a storm observed by Voyager 2 on Neptune in 1989.
astronomy-0299: Which is the only spacecraft to have visited the ice giants Uranus and Neptune, in 1986 and 1989?
Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989).
astronomy-0300: Which region of Pluto is nicknamed 'Pluto's heart' because of its shape?
Tombaugh Regio is Pluto's largest bright feature, nicknamed Pluto's heart for its shape.
astronomy-0301: What is the brightest asteroid visible from Earth?
Vesta is the brightest asteroid visible from Earth.
astronomy-0302: Which spacecraft orbited Vesta and then the dwarf planet Ceres after launching in September 2007?
NASA launched Dawn in September 2007 to study the asteroid belt's two largest bodies, Vesta and Ceres.
astronomy-0303: Which probe orbited Mercury between 2011 and 2015?
MESSENGER orbited Mercury between 2011 and 2015, studying its composition and magnetic field.
astronomy-0304: How did Magellan map Venus's surface in the 1990s despite its thick clouds?
Magellan used synthetic-aperture radar to map Venus's surface through its clouds.
astronomy-0305: Until which year did Opportunity operate on Mars after landing in 2004?
Opportunity operated on Mars from 2004 to 2018, about 14 years, although its planned mission was 90 days.
astronomy-0306: Which solar space observatory launched in December 1995 became the leading comet discoverer, finding over five thousand?
The SOHO solar observatory has discovered over 5000 comets since launch.
astronomy-0307: What was the main mission of Europe's Gaia observatory, operating between 2013 and 2025?
Searching for water on the Moon
Precisely measuring the positions and motions of about a billion stars
Gaia mapped the positions and motions of about a billion stars in our galaxy in three dimensions.
astronomy-0308: Which Chinese mission returned lunar surface samples to Earth in December 2020?
Chang'e 5 launched on 23 November 2020, collected about 1.7 kilograms of lunar soil, and returned it to Earth.
astronomy-0309: When was the uncrewed Artemis I mission around the Moon launched?
Artemis I launched on 16 November 2022 on an uncrewed test flight around the Moon.
astronomy-0310: When was the Tianhe core module of China's Tiangong space station launched?
Tianhe launched on 29 April 2021 as the first part of the Tiangong station.
astronomy-0311: What spacecraft carried the first Chinese astronaut, Yang Liwei, in October 2003?
Shenzhou 5 launched on 15 October 2003, the first human flight in China's space program.
astronomy-0312: Who was the first Indian in space, traveling aboard Soyuz T-11 in April 1984?
Rakesh Sharma traveled aboard Soyuz T-11 on 3 April 1984 under the Intercosmos program.
astronomy-0313: What was the Hubble Deep Field captured by the Hubble telescope in December 1995?
An image of a small patch of sky revealing thousands of distant galaxies
A complete map of the surface of Mars
The first image of Pluto's surface
An image of the first black hole
The Hubble Deep Field image combined 342 exposures taken between 18 and 28 December 1995, revealing about three thousand galaxies in a tiny area.
astronomy-0315: Which comet was the target of the European Rosetta mission launched in March 2004?
Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko was the target of Rosetta, launched on 2 March 2004.
astronomy-0316: From which asteroid did Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft return samples to Earth in December 2020?
Hayabusa2 encountered asteroid Ryugu in 2018 and returned its samples to Earth on 5 December 2020.
astronomy-0317: Which comet was struck by an impactor released from Deep Impact in 2005 to study its interior?
Deep Impact was designed to study the interior of comet Tempel 1 by releasing an impactor to strike it.
astronomy-0319: Which planet in the Solar System has the strongest magnetic field?
Jupiter has the strongest planetary magnetic field, generated by currents in the metallic hydrogen inside it.
earth-weather-0002: Earth's inner core remains solid despite its immense heat. Why?
It contains no iron or nickel
The iron at Earth's center is cold
It is far from heat sources in the mantle
The extreme pressure at Earth's center raises iron's melting point, keeping the inner core solid.
earth-weather-0003: Which Danish scientist discovered in 1936 that Earth has a solid inner core?
In 1936, Inge Lehmann inferred the existence of a solid inner core by analyzing seismic waves.
earth-weather-0004: What is the boundary between Earth's crust and mantle called?
The boundary between the crust and mantle was named after its Croatian discoverer, Andrija Mohorovicic, in 1909.
earth-weather-0005: The boundary between the mantle and outer core bears the name of which seismologist?
The boundary between the mantle and core is known as the Gutenberg discontinuity, after Beno Gutenberg.
earth-weather-0006: Which layer of Earth has the greatest volume?
The mantle makes up about 84% of Earth's volume, making it its largest layer.
earth-weather-0007: Which two metals dominate the composition of Earth's core?
Earth's core consists mainly of an iron-nickel alloy.
earth-weather-0008: What is the weak, deformable layer beneath the lithosphere over which tectonic plates slide?
The asthenosphere is a weak, deformable part of the upper mantle over which lithospheric plates move.
earth-weather-0011: What was the enormous global ocean surrounding the supercontinent Pangaea called?
Panthalassa was a giant ocean surrounding Pangaea; its name means 'all the sea'.
earth-weather-0013: Which ancient sea separated Laurasia from Gondwana, with the Mediterranean considered one of its remnants?
The Tethys Ocean lay between Laurasia and Gondwana; the Mediterranean, Black and Caspian seas are remnants of it.
earth-weather-0014: Which evidence did Wegener use to support continental drift?
The direction of trade winds over the ocean
Matching coastlines and fossils in Africa and South America
Rising sea levels during ice ages
Wegener noted matching coastlines and identical fossils on widely separated continents.
earth-weather-0015: Which American geologist proposed seafloor spreading in the early 1960s?
Harry Hess proposed that the seafloor is renewed at ridges and spreads sideways.
earth-weather-0017: Which island lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, exposing its rift above sea level?
Iceland is a part of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that rises above sea level.
earth-weather-0018: At which type of plate boundary do two plates slide horizontally past one another?
At a transform boundary, two plates move horizontally alongside each other without creating or consuming crust.
earth-weather-0019: Which famous American fault forms a transform boundary between the Pacific and North American plates?
California's San Andreas Fault is a transform boundary between the Pacific and North American plates.
earth-weather-0020: The Himalayas formed when the Indian Plate collided with which plate?
The Himalayas rose as a result of the Indian Plate colliding with the Eurasian Plate.
earth-weather-0022: In which ocean trench is Challenger Deep located?
Challenger Deep lies in the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific Ocean.
earth-weather-0023: Which region in East Africa is where three rifts meet: the Red Sea Rift, the Gulf of Aden Rift and the Great African Rift?
The Afar Triangle is a triple junction of the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and East African rifts.
earth-weather-0024: Geologically, the Red Sea formed as the Arabian Plate moved away from which plate?
The Red Sea is an expanding rift between the Arabian and African (Nubian) plates.
earth-weather-0025: Which mountain range formed from the collision of the Arabian and Eurasian plates?
The Zagros Mountains formed from the collision of the Arabian and Eurasian plates.
earth-weather-0027: What is the deepest hole humans have drilled into Earth's crust?
Russia's Kola borehole reached about 12.2 kilometers, making it the deepest artificial hole.
earth-weather-0028: Earth's age was estimated at about 4.54 billion years through radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest minerals.
earth-weather-0030: Earth's last complete magnetic pole reversal is named after two scientists. What is it called?
The last complete magnetic reversal was the Brunhes-Matuyama reversal, about 780 thousand years ago.
earth-weather-0031: According to scientists, what moves Earth's plates?
Mantle convection and the pull of sinking slabs
Plates move under forces from the mantle, chiefly slab pull, ridge push and convection currents.
earth-weather-0033: Which type of Earth's crust is denser and thinner?
Oceanic crust is basaltic, denser and thinner than the more granite-rich continental crust.
earth-weather-0035: Which earlier supercontinent preceded Pangaea and assembled about a billion years ago?
Rodinia was a supercontinent that assembled about 1.1 billion years ago and broke up long before Pangaea.
earth-weather-0036: Who mapped the Atlantic seafloor with her colleague Bruce Heezen, revealing the rift valley in its mid-ocean ridge?
Marie Tharp's maps revealed the rift valley in the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, supporting continental drift theory.
earth-weather-0038: How many major tectonic plates is Earth's crust usually divided into?
The lithosphere is divided into seven or eight major plates and a number of smaller ones.
earth-weather-0039: Which tectonic plate has the greatest area?
The Pacific Plate is the largest tectonic plate and consists mostly of oceanic crust.
earth-weather-0041: What is the long continental depression that forms when a continent begins to split and move apart?
A rift valley (graben) forms when continental crust stretches, fractures and its central block subsides.
earth-weather-0044: In which geological era did the supercontinent Pangaea begin to break apart?
Pangaea began breaking apart in the early Mesozoic Era, during the Jurassic Period.
earth-weather-0045: Which metamorphic rocks in Canada are among the oldest known rocks on Earth, at about 4 billion years old?
The Acasta Gneiss in Canada's Northwest Territories is among the oldest known rocks, at about 4 billion years old.
earth-weather-0046: Which mineral's grains found in Australia's Jack Hills are about 4.4 billion years old, making them the oldest known terrestrial materials?
Zircon grains in the Jack Hills are the oldest known terrestrial materials, at about 4.4 billion years old.
earth-weather-0047: Approximately how thick is continental crust?
Continental crust ranges from 25 to 70 kilometers thick, much thicker than oceanic crust.
earth-weather-0049: Why do secondary (S) waves not pass through Earth's outer core?
They are too fast for the core to absorb
The core's magnetism reflects them completely
The outer core is colder than the mantle
S waves are shear waves that cannot travel through liquids, and the outer core is liquid.
earth-weather-0050: What is the region on Earth's surface that direct seismic waves from a distant earthquake do not reach because they refract in the core?
Wave paths refract at the core, creating a seismic shadow zone where direct waves are not detected.
earth-weather-0052: Which scale do seismologists now use to measure the magnitude of large earthquakes instead of the Richter scale?
The moment magnitude scale replaced the Richter scale for estimating large earthquakes because of its accuracy.
earth-weather-0053: What does the Mercalli earthquake scale measure?
The length of the fault that slipped during the earthquake
The depth of the focus below Earth's surface
The total energy released from the earthquake's focus
The intensity of shaking and its effects on people and buildings
The Mercalli scale is an intensity scale describing the shaking people feel and the damage that occurs.
earth-weather-0054: For a one-unit increase in earthquake magnitude, by approximately what factor does the released energy increase?
Each one-unit increase in magnitude means about 32 times more energy.
earth-weather-0055: What is the strongest earthquake recorded by instruments to date?
The Valdivia earthquake (1960), with a magnitude of 9.4-9.6, is the strongest earthquake recorded by instruments.
earth-weather-0057: What happens to water-saturated sandy soil during strong seismic shaking?
It swells and rises above the surrounding ground
It loses its cohesion and behaves like a liquid
It quickly hardens into solid rock
It dries completely and cracks into small blocks
Liquefaction is a phenomenon in which saturated soil loses its rigidity due to shaking and behaves like a liquid.
earth-weather-0060: What natural sign may precede a tsunami reaching the shore?
Cold winds blow from the land
The sea suddenly recedes from the shore
Water may recede unusually far from the shore before the wave crest arrives.
earth-weather-0061: At approximately what speed does a tsunami wave travel in the deep ocean?
In the deep ocean, tsunamis travel at a jet plane's speed of about 800 km/h.
earth-weather-0062: In which year did a powerful earthquake strike the Indian Ocean floor near Sumatra, causing a massive tsunami?
The Indian Ocean earthquake and Sumatra tsunami occurred on 26 December 2004.
earth-weather-0063: On what day did the great Lisbon earthquake of 1755 occur?
The Lisbon earthquake occurred on the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day.
earth-weather-0064: Which seismic waves move the ground in a rolling circular motion resembling sea waves?
Rayleigh waves are surface waves that move the ground in a rolling elliptical motion like sea waves.
earth-weather-0065: Which theory explains earthquakes as stress accumulating in rocks on either side of a fault and then suddenly being released?
Harry Reid developed elastic rebound theory after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake.
earth-weather-0067: Which earthquake in 2011 caused the tsunami that led to the Fukushima nuclear power plant accident?
The 2011 Tohoku earthquake off Japan's coast generated a tsunami that struck the Fukushima plant.
earth-weather-0068: What is an earthquake at a subduction boundary between two plates called, a type that includes the world's strongest earthquakes?
Megathrust earthquakes occur at subduction boundaries and include the strongest recorded earthquakes.
earth-weather-0069: What is the inclined zone of earthquake foci that deepens with the descending plate in subduction zones called?
The Wadati-Benioff zone is an inclined plane of earthquake foci tracing the descending plate.
earth-weather-0070: What seismic activity can humans cause by injecting fluids underground or filling large dams?
Induced seismicity consists of earthquakes caused by human activities such as injection, mining and reservoir filling. Most are small, but some can be destructive.
earth-weather-0071: Which instrument records Earth's vibrations as a graph?
A seismograph records ground motion during earthquakes.
earth-weather-0072: What does it mean for an earthquake to be shallow-focus?
Its focus is less than 70 kilometers deep
Its shaking lasted no more than one second
Its magnitude is below 2 on the moment magnitude scale
It occurred beneath shallow water directly near the coast
Earthquakes are considered shallow if their focus is less than about 70 kilometers deep.
earth-weather-0074: Which Japanese scale describes shaking intensity in grades from 0 to 7?
The Japan Meteorological Agency uses the Shindo intensity scale, whose highest grade is 7.
earth-weather-0076: What activity at Saudi Arabia's Harrat Lunayyir in 2009 alarmed residents and led to thousands being evacuated?
A swarm of small earthquakes linked to magma
A volcanic eruption that flooded nearby villages with lava
A severe sandstorm lasting several continuous weeks
A flash flood that swept through valleys after heavy rain
In 2009, Harrat Lunayyir experienced an earthquake swarm caused by a magma dike intruding underground.
earth-weather-0077: Where do about 90% of the world's earthquakes occur?
About 90% of earthquakes occur along the Ring of Fire surrounding the Pacific Ocean.
earth-weather-0078: What is a fault called when its upper block drops relative to the lower block due to tension?
In a normal fault, the hanging wall drops as the crust extends.
earth-weather-0079: What happens at a reverse fault?
The upper block rises above the lower one due to compression
The blocks move horizontally without either rising or falling
Friction melts the rocks on either side of the fault
The blocks separate and move apart due to tension and extension
A reverse fault results from compression, causing the hanging wall to rise above the other block.
earth-weather-0080: Which measurement is used to calculate a station's distance from an earthquake and then locate it using three stations?
The number of aftershocks recorded on the first day
The strength of winds accompanying the earthquake at the station
The rise in water levels in wells near the station
The difference between the arrival times of P and S waves
A station's distance from an earthquake is calculated from the difference between P- and S-wave arrival times; three distances intersect at the epicenter.
earth-weather-0081: Which American city was devastated by an earthquake and subsequent fires in 1906?
The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and subsequent fires destroyed most of the city.
earth-weather-0082: Which Moroccan city was almost destroyed by an earthquake in 1960 and then rebuilt south of its old location?
The 1960 Agadir earthquake destroyed the city, which was rebuilt at a nearby site.
earth-weather-0084: What is a section of an active fault that has not experienced a major earthquake for a long time, which scientists expect to rupture in the future, called?
A seismic gap is a section of an active fault where stress has accumulated without a major earthquake for some time.
earth-weather-0085: Which surface seismic waves shake the ground horizontally from side to side?
Love waves are surface waves that move the ground horizontally, perpendicular to their direction of travel.
earth-weather-0086: What causes most major earthquakes on Earth?
Strong winds pressing against high mountain slopes
Surface rocks expanding in intense sunlight
Earthquakes usually result from rocks rupturing and suddenly slipping along faults, releasing stored energy.
earth-weather-0087: What is the science studying earthquakes and the propagation of elastic waves inside Earth called?
Seismology studies earthquakes and the propagation of elastic waves through Earth.
earth-weather-0088: Which relationship states that small earthquakes occur more frequently than large ones according to a fixed logarithmic ratio?
The Gutenberg-Richter law relates earthquake magnitude to the number of occurrences in a region.
earth-weather-0089: Which law describes the declining number of aftershocks over time after a main earthquake?
Omori's law states that the aftershock rate decreases approximately in inverse proportion to time.
earth-weather-0090: According to US Geological Survey estimates, how many earthquakes of magnitude 7 or above occur worldwide each year on average?
Based on records since about 1900, the agency estimates about 15 major earthquakes (7-7.9) and one great earthquake (8 or above) worldwide each year.
earth-weather-0091: Which earthquake destroyed Tokyo and Yokohama in 1923?
The 1923 Great Kanto earthquake struck the Kanto Plain and devastated Tokyo and Yokohama.
earth-weather-0092: What is the difference between magma and lava?
Magma is underground; lava is magma that reaches the surface
Magma is solid rock; lava is molten rock
Lava forms in the core and magma in the crust
Magma is always much colder than lava
Molten rock is called magma while below the surface; once it emerges, it is called lava.
earth-weather-0093: What is basaltic lava with a smooth, undulating surface resembling twisted ropes called?
Pahoehoe lava has a smooth, undulating or ropy surface; its name comes from Hawaiian.
earth-weather-0094: What is lava with a rough, broken surface of sharp rock fragments called?
Aa lava has a rough surface of sharp, broken blocks.
earth-weather-0095: What shape does lava take when it flows underwater and cools rapidly?
Lava flowing underwater cools quickly, forming rounded masses called pillow lava.
earth-weather-0096: What is the tall, cone-shaped volcano made of alternating layers of lava and ash, such as Mount Fuji, called?
Mount Fuji is a stratovolcano made of successive layers of solidified lava and ash.
earth-weather-0098: 1816 was called the 'Year Without a Summer'. Which volcanic eruption was its main cause?
Tambora's 1815 eruption spread volcanic aerosols through the atmosphere, lowering global temperatures in 1816.
earth-weather-0099: The explosion of this volcano in 1883 was heard thousands of kilometers away and ranked among the loudest sounds in recorded history. Which volcano was it?
The 1883 Krakatoa explosion was heard in places thousands of kilometers away.
earth-weather-0100: Which volcanic eruption in 1991 lowered Earth's average temperature by about half a degree Celsius?
Pinatubo's 1991 eruption released immense quantities of sulfur aerosols, cooling Earth by about 0.5 degrees.
earth-weather-0101: What distinguished the 1980 eruption of America's Mount St. Helens?
Its flank collapsed in a huge landslide followed by a lateral blast
An eruption beneath ice caused a flood
A slow lava flow lasted a century
A new island appeared in the sea
The northern flank of Mount St. Helens collapsed in the largest recorded landslide, followed by a lateral blast.
earth-weather-0102: A violent explosive eruption with a towering ash column is named after a Roman writer who described the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE. What is it called?
Plinian eruptions are named after Pliny the Younger, who described the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE.
earth-weather-0103: In which type of eruption does a volcano eject glowing pieces of lava at short, regular intervals?
A Strombolian eruption is a series of short explosions ejecting glowing lava fragments, named after Stromboli volcano.
earth-weather-0105: Which volcanic rock floats on water because it contains so many bubbles?
Pumice is a spongy volcanic rock full of voids, giving it a lower density than water.
earth-weather-0106: Which black, glassy volcanic rock was used in the past to make sharp blades?
Obsidian is natural volcanic glass that cools rapidly and breaks with extremely sharp edges.
earth-weather-0107: What is an opening in the ground near volcanoes that emits hot gases and steam called?
A fumarole is an opening in the crust that emits volcanic steam and gases.
earth-weather-0110: Which famous geyser in Yellowstone National Park is known for its regular eruptions?
Yellowstone's Old Faithful geyser is famous for the regularity of its eruptions.
earth-weather-0111: Which volcano is considered the world's tallest mountain when measured from its base on the ocean floor to its summit?
Mauna Kea in Hawaii rises more than 10 thousand meters from its base on the ocean floor.
earth-weather-0112: What type of mountain is Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain?
A folded mountain of sedimentary rocks
Kilimanjaro is a dormant stratovolcano with three cones.
earth-weather-0113: Which Mexican volcano began emerging in a farmer's cornfield in 1943, allowing scientists to witness its birth and growth?
Paricutin volcano suddenly emerged in a cornfield in 1943 and grew rapidly.
earth-weather-0114: Which volcanic island emerged from the sea south of Iceland between 1963 and 1967 and became a laboratory for studying the colonization of life?
Surtsey formed from a submarine eruption between 1963 and 1967; scientists study how organisms colonize it.
earth-weather-0115: Which Icelandic volcano disrupted European air travel for weeks in 2010 with its ash cloud?
Ash from Eyjafjallajokull's 2010 eruption caused widespread closures of European airspace.
