earth-weather-0116: Which volcanic gas is most abundant in volcanic emissions?
Water vapor is the most abundant component of volcanic gases, followed by carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide.
earth-weather-0117: Which volcano in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is famous for one of the world's largest lava lakes?
Mount Nyiragongo contains one of the world's largest active lava lakes.
earth-weather-0118: Which volcano, on the border between Chile and Argentina, is the highest on Earth?
Ojos del Salado is the world's highest volcano at about 6893 meters.
earth-weather-0119: Which volcano in Antarctica contains a persistent lava lake?
Erebus is Antarctica's most active volcano, with a persistent lava lake in its crater.
earth-weather-0120: Which enormous eruption occurred in Sumatra about 74 thousand years ago, leaving the world's largest volcanic lake?
The immense Toba eruption about 74 thousand years ago left the volcanic Lake Toba.
earth-weather-0121: Which enormous basalt plateau in India formed from vast lava flows near the end of the age of dinosaurs?
The Deccan Traps are one of the largest volcanic provinces, formed about 66 million years ago.
earth-weather-0122: The great basalt flows of the Siberian Traps are linked to which event in the history of life?
The emergence of the first flowering plants
The end of the last ice age
Scientists link the Siberian Traps eruptions to the end-Permian extinction, the largest extinction in Earth's history.
earth-weather-0123: What is a small, steep volcanic cone made of solidified lava fragments around a single vent called?
A cinder cone is a small hill where frozen lava fragments accumulate around a single vent.
earth-weather-0124: Over what period did a series of eruptions form the basaltic lava fields of Harrat Khaybar north of Madinah?
The basalt fields of Harrat Khaybar formed through successive eruptions over about five million years.
earth-weather-0125: A volcanic eruption occurred in Harrat Rahat near Madinah in the seventh Hijri century. In which Gregorian year was it?
A volcano erupted in Harrat Rahat southeast of Madinah in 1256 CE (654 AH).
earth-weather-0126: Which Yemeni volcano on a Red Sea island erupted in 2007 after a long period of dormancy?
Jabal al-Tair is a volcanic island in the Red Sea that erupted in 2007.
earth-weather-0127: Which Ethiopian volcano in the Danakil Depression is known as the 'smoking mountain' and has a lava lake in its crater?
Erta Ale volcano in Afar contains a lava lake; its name means 'smoking mountain'.
earth-weather-0128: Which Ethiopian area is famous for hot springs colored yellow and green and sulfurous ground?
Dallol in the Danakil Depression is famous for hot springs and brightly colored salt and sulfur deposits.
earth-weather-0129: What is the material a volcano ejects into the air, including ash, fragments and rock blocks, called?
Tephra is the general name for all solid ejecta from an eruption, such as ash, cinders and blocks.
earth-weather-0130: What makes some volcanic eruptions violently explosive?
The volcano being near the equator
Low gas content in the magma
Viscous, silica-rich magma traps gases, allowing pressure to accumulate and then explode.
earth-weather-0131: Which Italian volcano on a small island is nicknamed the 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean' for its almost continuous eruptions?
Stromboli has erupted continuously for thousands of years, earning it the nickname 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean'.
earth-weather-0132: What is an eruption in which groundwater suddenly turns to steam when heated by magma and explodes without releasing new magma called?
A phreatic eruption is a steam explosion caused by magma heating groundwater.
earth-weather-0133: On which Indonesian island is Mount Tambora located?
Mount Tambora is on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa.
earth-weather-0134: Which instruments or methods do scientists use to monitor volcanoes and forecast eruptions?
Monitoring the direction of bird migration
Measuring the salinity of nearby seawater
Tracking small earthquakes, ground swelling and gases
Seismic activity, ground deformation and gas emissions are monitored to forecast eruptions.
earth-weather-0135: Which 1783 eruption in Iceland lasted eight months along long fissures and released toxic gases that killed large numbers of livestock?
The Laki fissure eruption (1783-1784) released fluorine and sulfur gases that killed most of Iceland's livestock.
earth-weather-0136: Which light, porous rock forms when volcanic ash is compacted and consolidated?
Tuff is a volcanic rock formed from consolidated volcanic ash.
earth-weather-0137: Which Colombian town was destroyed by a lahar resulting from the 1985 eruption of Nevado del Ruiz?
A lahar from Nevado del Ruiz buried the town of Armero in 1985.
earth-weather-0139: Through evaporation of saline lake water
Through transformation by heat and pressure without melting
Through cooling and solidification of magma or lava
Through accumulation of shells and sand on the seabed
Igneous rock forms when magma or lava cools and crystallizes.
earth-weather-0140: Why are granite crystals large enough to see with the naked eye?
It formed on the ocean floor
It cooled rapidly on Earth's surface
It cooled slowly deep inside Earth
Granite is an intrusive rock that cooled slowly below the surface, allowing large crystals to grow.
earth-weather-0142: What phenomenon formed the famous hexagonal columns of the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland?
Clay deposition on an ancient riverbed
Accumulation of salt crystals in lakes
Basalt fracturing as it cooled and contracted
The Giant's Causeway columns formed when basaltic lava fractured as it cooled and contracted.
earth-weather-0143: From what rock does marble form?
Limestone transformed by heat and pressure
Marble is a metamorphic rock formed through recrystallization of limestone or dolomite.
earth-weather-0144: Which metamorphic rock forms from shale and is used as slabs for roofing houses?
Slate is a fine-grained metamorphic rock formed from shale that splits into slabs.
earth-weather-0146: Which metamorphic rock is distinguished by alternating light and dark mineral bands?
Gneiss is a high-grade metamorphic rock distinguished by alternating bands of color.
earth-weather-0147: How do sedimentary rocks usually form?
Through sediments accumulating and consolidating in layers
Through rocks melting in the mantle
Through rocks transforming under intense pressure
Through lava cooling on the surface
Sedimentary rock forms when grains or organic materials are deposited and then consolidated.
earth-weather-0149: How does breccia differ from conglomerate?
It consists only of salt crystals
Its grains are smaller than clay particles
Its fragments are angular rather than rounded
Breccia consists of cemented angular rock fragments.
earth-weather-0150: Which is the main mineral in limestone?
Limestone consists mainly of calcium carbonate minerals such as calcite and aragonite.
earth-weather-0151: What is the origin of most naturally occurring limestone?
Remains of marine organisms' skeletons and shells
Most limestone forms from accumulated skeletal remains of marine organisms.
earth-weather-0152: Soft white chalk consists of the remains of which microscopic marine organisms?
Chalk is a soft limestone made of calcareous plates from microscopic algae called coccolithophores.
earth-weather-0153: Which hard siliceous sedimentary rock did early humans use to make tools and start fires?
Flint is a hard siliceous rock that breaks with sharp edges and produces sparks.
earth-weather-0155: What is the softest mineral on the Mohs hardness scale?
Talc is the softest mineral on the Mohs scale, with a rating of 1.
earth-weather-0156: What is quartz's rating on the Mohs hardness scale?
Quartz has a Mohs hardness of 7 and can scratch glass.
earth-weather-0157: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 9 and includes ruby and sapphire?
Corundum has a Mohs hardness of 9; ruby and sapphire are varieties of it.
earth-weather-0158: To which mineral does the gemstone emerald belong?
Emerald is a variety of beryl, colored green by chromium or vanadium.
earth-weather-0159: Which mineral is considered the most abundant in Earth's crust?
Feldspar minerals make up about 41% of the continental crust, making them its most abundant minerals.
earth-weather-0160: Which mineral splits into thin, transparent, flexible sheets?
Mica has perfect basal cleavage, splitting into thin, flexible sheets.
earth-weather-0161: Which mineral is known as 'fool's gold' because its color resembles the luster of gold?
Pyrite (iron sulfide) is nicknamed fool's gold because of its yellow metallic luster.
earth-weather-0163: What is the main ore from which aluminum is extracted?
Bauxite is the world's main source of aluminum.
earth-weather-0164: What is the main ore of lead, distinguished by shiny gray cubic crystals?
Galena (lead sulfide) is the most important lead ore.
earth-weather-0165: Which mineral makes up rock salt used as table salt?
Halite is the mineral form of sodium chloride, or rock salt.
earth-weather-0166: Which mineral is used to make plaster and has a Mohs hardness of 2?
Gypsum is a hydrated calcium sulfate mineral with a hardness of 2 and is used to make plaster.
earth-weather-0167: A desert rose is a rose-shaped crystal formation common in Gulf sands. Which mineral does it usually consist of?
Desert roses are clusters of gypsum or barite crystals containing sand grains.
earth-weather-0168: Which test involves rubbing a mineral on an unglazed porcelain plate to determine the color of its powder?
Streak is the color of a mineral's powder on a porcelain plate, which is more consistent than the mineral's own color.
earth-weather-0169: What is a hollow rock lined inside with crystals such as quartz or amethyst called?
A geode is a hollow rock lined with crystals on the inside.
earth-weather-0170: What are stalactites in limestone caves?
Small lakes on the cave floor
Formations hanging from the cave ceiling
Formations rising from the cave floor
Stalactites are calcareous deposits hanging from the ceiling, while stalagmites rise from the floor.
earth-weather-0171: Which organic sedimentary rock formed from plant remains buried millions of years ago?
Coal is a combustible sedimentary rock formed through accumulation and transformation of plant remains.
earth-weather-0172: What is amber, in which ancient insects are sometimes preserved?
Amber is fossilized tree resin that may preserve ancient insects inside it.
earth-weather-0173: How does wood become petrified wood?
Minerals gradually replace the organic material
Wood dries in the desert for thousands of years
Wood burns and then suddenly cools
In petrified wood, minerals such as silica replace the wood tissue while preserving its structure.
earth-weather-0175: What are fossils used to date and correlate rock layers because they existed briefly but were widespread called?
Index fossils are used to date and correlate rock layers.
earth-weather-0177: Which marine fossils have coiled spiral shells and lived until the end of the age of dinosaurs?
Ammonites were cephalopods with coiled shells that became extinct along with the dinosaurs.
earth-weather-0178: What are stromatolites, among the oldest traces of life on Earth?
Stromatolites are layered sedimentary structures built by colonies of cyanobacteria.
earth-weather-0180: Which limestone precipitates from hot springs and was an important Roman building material?
Travertine is a limestone deposited by spring water; it was used to build the Colosseum.
earth-weather-0182: Which blue-green gemstone were Iran and Sinai famous for in ancient times?
Turquoise is a blue-green mineral mined in Sinai and Iran since ancient times.
earth-weather-0183: Which olive-green gemstone is a variety of the mineral olivine?
Peridot is a gem variety of the mineral olivine.
earth-weather-0185: What causes thin layers to peel off granite surfaces like onion skins?
Rock minerals dissolving in infiltrating acidic rainwater
Windblown sand grains eroding the exposed rock surface
Plant roots growing in rock cracks and widening them over time
Rock expanding and contracting with temperature changes and pressure release
Exfoliation occurs as sheets separate from the rock surface due to pressure release and thermal expansion and contraction.
earth-weather-0187: Which sand dune has multiple arms branching from a central peak and forms when winds blow from different directions?
A star dune is pyramidal with multiple arms and forms under winds of changing directions.
earth-weather-0188: What is desert pavement, or reg?
A vast sea of sand dunes moving with prevailing winds
A surface covered with closely packed pebbles after wind removes fine sand
A desert depression where groundwater emerges and palm trees grow
A dry salt lake whose crust cracks in the hot summer
Desert pavement is a surface of tightly packed pebbles remaining after wind blows away fine particles.
earth-weather-0189: What is the dark, shiny layer that coats desert rocks over long periods?
A film of green algae and lichens
Desert varnish is a dark film of manganese and iron oxides and clay covering exposed rocks.
earth-weather-0190: What is a sabkha, known along the Arabian Gulf coast?
A flat coastal plain covered with a salt crust
A tall sand hill surrounding an oasis
A deep valley carrying floods after rain
A sabkha is a coastal or inland salt flat where salt forms through evaporation.
earth-weather-0192: Why is a river delta given this name?
It is the name of a city at the Nile's mouth
It is the name of its first discoverer
Its shape resembles the Greek letter delta
Herodotus compared the triangular Nile Delta to the Greek letter delta.
earth-weather-0194: Which river carved the Grand Canyon in the United States?
The Colorado River carved Arizona's Grand Canyon over millions of years.
earth-weather-0195: What is the cross-sectional shape of a valley carved by a glacier?
Glaciers carve U-shaped valleys, while rivers carve V-shaped valleys.
earth-weather-0196: What is the semicircular basin carved by ice at the head of a mountain valley called?
A cirque is a semicircular, amphitheater-like basin carved by a glacier high on a mountain.
earth-weather-0197: What is an elongated oval hill of glacial deposits resembling an upside-down spoon called?
A drumlin is an oval hill of glacial deposits elongated in the direction of ice movement.
earth-weather-0198: What is a long, winding ridge of sand and gravel deposited by water flowing through tunnels beneath ice called?
An esker is a ridge of sand and gravel deposited in water channels beneath or within glaciers.
earth-weather-0199: What is a large rock transported far from its origin by ice and left on ground with different rocks called?
Rock balanced on a narrow base
A glacial erratic is a rock transported by ice that differs from the rocks where it came to rest.
earth-weather-0200: Approximately how much of a floating iceberg's volume is underwater?
Because ice has a density close to that of seawater, about 90% of an iceberg's volume is submerged.
earth-weather-0201: What is the breaking off of ice masses from a glacier's edge and their falling into the sea called?
Ice calving is the separation of blocks from a glacier's edge to become icebergs.
earth-weather-0202: When did ice sheets reach their greatest extent during the last ice age?
The last ice age reached its peak (the Last Glacial Maximum) about 26 to 20 thousand years ago.
earth-weather-0203: What is a natural sinkhole filled with groundwater in Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula called?
A cenote is a sinkhole in limestone exposing groundwater; cenotes are common in Yucatan.
earth-weather-0204: Which weak acid slowly dissolves limestone, forming caves?
Carbonic acid from carbon dioxide dissolving in water
Sulfuric acid seeping from nearby volcanic emissions
Nitric acid formed in the air by lightning and storms
Acetic acid formed by fermentation of plant remains in soil
Carbon dioxide dissolves in rainwater to form carbonic acid, which dissolves limestone.
earth-weather-0205: What is a hoodoo in a rocky desert?
A tall, thin rock pillar often capped by harder rock
A crescent sand dune slowly moving with the wind
A narrow underground cave cut into limestone by groundwater
A temporary salt lake filled by floods that dries in summer
A hoodoo is a thin rock pillar sculpted by erosion, often protected by harder rock at its top.
earth-weather-0206: How does a butte differ from a mesa in desert terrain?
A butte has a smaller area than a mesa, though both have flat tops
A butte is coastal, while a mesa is high in the mountains
A butte is taller than a mesa and has a pointed conical summit
A butte consists of loose sand, while a mesa is solid rock
A butte is an isolated, steep-sided hill with a flat top, smaller in area than a mesa.
earth-weather-0207: What is an isolated rock pillar in the sea near the coast, sculpted by waves, called?
A sea stack is an isolated rock pillar near the shore left after a sea arch collapses.
earth-weather-0208: What is the strongest factor sculpting desert rocks into mushroom shapes?
Rising groundwater saturating the rock's base
Ancient glaciers that passed through the area
Repeated heavy rainfall on the rock's top
Sand-laden winds erode the lower part of a rock more than its top, giving it a mushroom shape.
earth-weather-0209: Rounded river gravel accumulated in dry valley beds
Green marine clay deposited in ancient lake beds
Fine yellowish silt deposits carried by wind
Black porous volcanic rock formed by cooling lava
Loess consists of fine windblown silt deposits that form fertile soil.
earth-weather-0210: What is the dark organic component of soil resulting from decomposition of plant and animal remains?
Humus is decomposed organic matter that darkens soil and increases its fertility.
earth-weather-0211: What are the distinct horizontal layers visible in a soil profile called?
A soil profile consists of distinct horizons (layers) designated by letters.
earth-weather-0212: What is the red soil rich in iron and aluminum oxides found in humid tropical regions called?
Laterite is soil rich in iron and aluminum that forms through intense weathering in hot, humid regions.
earth-weather-0213: What is the highly fertile black soil widespread in the steppes of Ukraine and Russia called?
Chernozem is black, humus-rich soil; its Russian name means 'black earth'.
earth-weather-0214: What is a flash flood that occurs in desert valleys?
A high sea wave reaching the coast after an underwater earthquake
A sudden rise in water within a few hours of heavy rain
Groundwater rising until it floods the valley surface
A slow, gradual flood lasting months after snowmelt
A flash flood is a sudden rise in water in valleys within about six hours of heavy rain.
earth-weather-0215: What is usually the water source in desert oases?
Groundwater reaching or nearing the surface
Dewdrops collecting on sand during cold winter nights
Melting snow on mountains surrounding the desert
Seawater seeping beneath sand into inland depressions
Oases usually depend on groundwater in water-bearing layers.
earth-weather-0217: A well whose water rises under natural pressure and may flow without pumping
A well near the sea with salty water
A dry well filled with rainwater in winter
A hand-dug well from which buckets are lifted
An artesian well penetrates a confined, pressurized aquifer, causing water to rise without pumping.
earth-weather-0218: What is the world's largest known fossil groundwater reservoir, lying beneath Egypt, Libya, Sudan and Chad?
The great Rub al-Khali groundwater basin
Dammam limestone aquifer in eastern Arabia
The Nubian Sandstone Aquifer System is the largest known fossil groundwater reservoir.
earth-weather-0219: Which cave is considered the world's longest known cave system?
Son Doong Cave in central Vietnam
Mammoth Cave in the United States
Jeita Grotto in Lebanon's Nahr al-Kalb valley
Mammoth Cave in Kentucky is the longest known cave system, extending over 680 kilometers.
earth-weather-0220: What is the world's largest known cave passage by volume?
Deep Voronya Cave in the Caucasus Mountains
Son Doong Cave in Vietnam is the largest known natural cave by volume.
earth-weather-0221: In which valley is Lebanon's Jeita Grotto, famous for its stalactites and stalagmites?
Jeita Grotto is in the Nahr al-Kalb valley north of Beirut.
earth-weather-0222: What is a landslide in Earth science?
Rock or soil masses sliding down a slope under gravity
An oceanic plate descending beneath a continental plate at trenches
Sand dunes advancing over roads and farms in strong winds
Clay ground cracking during prolonged summer drought
A landslide is the movement of rock, soil or debris masses down a slope.
earth-weather-0223: Which vast salt flats in Bolivia are considered the largest in the world?
Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni is the world's largest salt flat.
earth-weather-0224: What is wind's lifting and removal of sand and fine dust from Earth's surface called?
Deflation is the removal of fine particles from Earth's surface by wind.
earth-weather-0225: Which mountains form when rock layers bend under compression as plates collide?
Fold mountains form through compression folding rock layers, as in the Himalayas and Alps.
earth-weather-0226: Which glacier is considered the world's longest outside the polar regions?
Aletsch Glacier in the Swiss Alps
Fedchenko Glacier in the Pamir Mountains is the longest glacier outside the polar regions.
earth-weather-0227: Which sand dune has arms pointing upwind, with vegetation anchoring its ends?
In a parabolic dune, vegetation anchors the arms, causing them to point against the wind direction.
earth-weather-0228: What is a hamada in the Sahara?
A fertile oasis with many palm trees and springs
A barren rocky plateau with little sand
A vast sand sea of moving dunes
A dry salt lake covered in a white crust
A hamada is an elevated rocky desert surface from which wind has removed most of the sand.
earth-weather-0229: In which atmospheric layer is most of the ozone layer found?
The ozone layer lies in the lower stratosphere at an altitude of about 15-35 kilometers.
earth-weather-0231: Which boundary at an altitude of 100 kilometers above sea level is widely used as the start of outer space?
The Karman line at an altitude of 100 km is widely used as the boundary between the atmosphere and space.
earth-weather-0232: What is the approximate average atmospheric pressure at sea level?
Average atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 1013.25 hectopascals.
earth-weather-0233: Who invented the mercury barometer to measure atmospheric pressure in 1643?
Torricelli invented the mercury barometer in 1643.
earth-weather-0234: Which instrument measures wind speed at weather stations?
earth-weather-0235: A hygrometer is an instrument for measuring air humidity.
earth-weather-0236: What is the white wooden box with sloping slats that houses thermometers at weather stations called?
A Stevenson screen protects instruments from sun and rain while allowing air to pass through.
earth-weather-0237: What is the temperature to which air must cool to become saturated with water vapor and begin condensation called?
The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated and its vapor condenses.
earth-weather-0239: Which English chemist introduced Latin names for cloud types, such as cumulus, stratus and cirrus, in 1802?
In 1802, Luke Howard proposed a cloud classification using Latin names still in use today.
earth-weather-0240: What are the high, thin, white, feathery clouds made of ice crystals called?
Cirrus clouds are high, thin, feathery clouds made of ice crystals.
earth-weather-0241: What are the giant thunderclouds with flat, anvil-shaped tops called?
Cumulonimbus clouds are huge vertical clouds associated with thunderstorms, with anvil-shaped tops.
earth-weather-0242: What does the Latin component 'nimbus' mean in cloud names?
The word nimbus indicates a rain-bearing cloud.
earth-weather-0244: What are the white trails jet aircraft leave in the sky?
Airborne dust stirred by the aircraft's wings
Smoke from fuel burning in the engines
Condensation trails from engine exhaust vapor
Colored gases released to mark the aircraft's route for observers
These trails form when water vapor in engine exhaust condenses and freezes.
earth-weather-0245: What is the best-known substance used in cloud seeding to encourage rainfall?
Silver iodide is the best-known cloud-seeding material because it resembles ice crystals.
earth-weather-0246: What is the actual shape of a large raindrop as it falls?
Rounded on top and flattened underneath
A teardrop pointed at the top and rounded underneath
A short cylinder elongated in the direction of falling
A perfect sphere at every size
Large raindrops flatten underneath due to air resistance; they are not teardrop-shaped.
earth-weather-0247: How many sides does a typical snow crystal have?
A snowflake crystallizes with sixfold symmetry because of the arrangement of water molecules in the ice crystal.
earth-weather-0248: Supercooled droplets that freeze on contact with surfaces
Dew freezing on grass at night
Freezing rain falls as supercooled liquid and freezes immediately on contact with surfaces.
earth-weather-0249: What is the frost covering grass on cold, clear nights?
Tiny snowflakes falling from low clouds late at night
Ice crystals forming directly from water vapor on cold surfaces
Drizzle droplets freezing in the air before landing on grass
Dewdrops forming first and then slowly freezing after midnight
Frost forms when water vapor turns directly into ice on a surface below freezing.
earth-weather-0250: Approximately how hot is a lightning channel?
A lightning channel heats to about 30 thousand degrees, hotter than the Sun's surface.
earth-weather-0251: What causes the sound of thunder?
Heavy clouds colliding in the atmosphere
Sudden expansion of air heated by lightning
Water vapor trapped in the thundercloud exploding
Large hailstones falling onto building roofs
Lightning suddenly heats air, causing it to expand rapidly and generate the sound wave called thunder.
earth-weather-0252: What is the glowing blue light sometimes seen on ship masts and the tips of pointed objects during storms?
St. Elmo's fire is a glowing electrical discharge around pointed objects in electrically charged air.
earth-weather-0253: Which phenomenon deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere due to Earth's rotation?
The Coriolis effect arising from Earth's rotation deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
earth-weather-0255: What does force 12 on the Beaufort scale mean?
The highest grade on the Beaufort scale is 12, meaning hurricane-force winds.
earth-weather-0256: Which scale classifies Atlantic tropical cyclones into categories 1 to 5?
The Saffir-Simpson scale classifies tropical cyclones into five categories according to wind speed.
earth-weather-0257: What is a tropical cyclone called if it forms in the northwestern Pacific Ocean?
A tropical cyclone in the northwestern Pacific is called a typhoon; in the Atlantic, it is called a hurricane.
earth-weather-0258: In which direction do winds rotate around a low-pressure system in the Northern Hemisphere?
Clockwise in summer and counterclockwise in winter
They do not rotate but blow in a straight line
Winds rotate counterclockwise around a low-pressure system in the Northern Hemisphere because of the Coriolis force.
earth-weather-0259: What weather usually accompanies a high-pressure system?
Clear skies and stable descending air
Dense cumuliform clouds and hail showers
In a high-pressure system, air descends, warms and dries, usually producing clear skies.
earth-weather-0260: What usually happens when a cold front passes over an area?
A sudden large rise in both temperature and humidity
A temperature drop with rain showers and sometimes thunder
Dense fog lasting a week without rain
Calm winds for days with completely clear skies
Cold air pushes warm air upward, forming cumuliform clouds and showers, followed by falling temperatures.
earth-weather-0261: Why does a sea breeze blow toward the coast during the day?
Land heats faster than water, lowering the pressure above it
Trade winds reverse direction at noon
The sea heats faster than land, increasing its pressure by day
The Moon's gravity pushes air toward the shore at high tide
Land heats faster than the sea during the day, making air rise and pressure fall above it, so air moves toward it from the sea.
earth-weather-0262: What is a jet stream in the atmosphere?
A column of hot air rising above active volcanoes
Steady surface winds blowing near the equator throughout the year
A warm ocean current flowing beneath the Atlantic surface
A narrow, fast air current in the upper troposphere
Jet streams are narrow, fast rivers of air near the tropopause, usually flowing from west to east.
earth-weather-0264: What are the horse latitudes in the global wind system?
Strong westerly wind belts near latitude 50 in both hemispheres
A rainy equatorial region where trade winds meet
A belt of cold polar winds near the polar circles
The horse latitudes are subtropical belts near 30 degrees north and south, with light winds and high pressure.
earth-weather-0265: What are the warm, dry winds descending on sheltered mountain slopes, known by a particular name in the Alps?
Foehn winds are warm, dry air descending on the leeward side of mountains.
earth-weather-0267: What is a haboob, common in Sudan and hot deserts?
Sudden heavy rain without wind or thunder
Cold winds descending from mountains on winter nights
Dense coastal fog covering coastal cities in the morning
A dense wall of dust carried by thunderstorm downdrafts or frontal winds
A haboob is a dense dust wall that may be raised by thunderstorm downdrafts or winds along a weather front.
earth-weather-0268: Which hot, dusty spring winds blow over Egypt and have a name associated with a number of days?
Khamsin winds are hot, dry and dusty winds over Egypt; their name is associated with about fifty days.
earth-weather-0269: What are the hot winds blowing from the Sahara across the Mediterranean toward southern Europe called?
The sirocco is a hot wind originating in the Sahara and blowing toward southern Europe.
earth-weather-0270: What are the cold northerly winds blowing across southern France toward the Mediterranean called?
The mistral is a strong, cold northerly wind blowing through the Rhone Valley toward the Mediterranean.
earth-weather-0272: What was the first successful weather satellite, launched in 1960?
TIROS-1 was the first successful weather satellite, launched in April 1960.
earth-weather-0273: Where is the headquarters of the World Meteorological Organization?
The World Meteorological Organization is a UN agency headquartered in Geneva.
earth-weather-0274: Which British naval officer established Britain's first meteorological service and coined the term 'weather forecast'?
Robert FitzRoy founded Britain's Met Office and coined the term 'forecast'.
earth-weather-0275: Which Norwegian scientist founded the Bergen School in 1917, establishing many foundations of modern weather forecasting?
Vilhelm Bjerknes founded the Bergen School of meteorology in 1917 with his younger colleagues.
earth-weather-0276: Which scientist became known for the butterfly effect after discovering weather models' sensitivity to small changes?
Edward Lorenz discovered that tiny changes in input could completely alter forecasts and formulated the butterfly-effect analogy.
earth-weather-0277: Which radar measures the movement of raindrops toward or away from it to detect storm rotation?
Doppler radar uses the Doppler effect to measure the speed of precipitation toward or away from the radar.
earth-weather-0279: What is the basic difference between weather and climate?
Weather concerns the atmosphere over seas, while climate concerns it over land
Climate is the average weather over a long period of around thirty years
Weather is measured only by satellites, while climate is measured by ground stations
Climate describes the atmosphere at a particular hour, while weather describes it over centuries
Weather is the state of the atmosphere over a short time; climate is average weather over a long period, traditionally 30 years.
earth-weather-0281: In the Koppen classification, which group includes Kuwait's hot desert climate?
Dry climates in the Koppen classification use the symbol B, including the hot desert climate BWh.
earth-weather-0282: What is the highest temperature recorded in Kuwait, observed at Mitribah in 2016?
Mitribah station recorded about 54 degrees Celsius on 21 July 2016; the World Meteorological Organization certified the value as 53.9 degrees.
earth-weather-0283: Where was Earth's lowest naturally measured surface temperature, about -89.2 degrees Celsius, recorded?
Mount Everest's summit in the Himalayas
Oymyakon village in eastern Siberia, Russia
North Ice station in central Greenland
Russia's Vostok Station recorded -89.2 degrees in 1983, the lowest meteorologically measured temperature.
earth-weather-0284: Which Indian town is among the world's wettest places by annual average rainfall?
Mawsynram in Meghalaya is famous for the highest recorded annual average rainfall.
earth-weather-0285: What is the proportion of incoming sunlight reflected by a surface called?
Albedo measures a surface's reflectivity; fresh snow has a high albedo and the ocean a low one.
earth-weather-0286: Which natural surface reflects the most sunlight?
Fresh snow reflects most sunlight, while the ocean reflects only a small portion.
earth-weather-0287: Why are large cities warmer than the surrounding countryside, especially at night?
Air humidity is much higher in cities and prevents cooling
Monsoon winds avoid passing over built-up areas
Their buildings and asphalt absorb and store heat
Cities are usually at lower elevations than the countryside
This is called the urban heat island effect, caused by buildings and pavements absorbing heat and by limited vegetation.
earth-weather-0288: What do ice cores extracted from Antarctica preserve that helps reveal past climates?
Air bubbles trapped from ancient times
Volcanic mineral crystals revealing the number of past earthquakes
Remains of tropical plants frozen millions of years ago
Ancient salty seawater trapped between ice layers
Ice layers trap bubbles of past air, revealing the atmosphere's former composition and temperature.
earth-weather-0290: What was the Little Ice Age?
A widespread ice age when ice sheets covered Europe twenty thousand years ago
A relatively cold period extending roughly from the fourteenth to the nineteenth century
A short cold period lasting two years after Pinatubo's 1991 eruption
Only a series of harsh European winters during World War I
The Little Ice Age was a period of regional cooling, especially in the Northern Hemisphere, roughly between the 14th and 19th centuries.
earth-weather-0291: Who linked successive ice ages to periodic changes in Earth's orbit and axial tilt?
Milankovitch cycles are orbital changes affecting the distribution of sunlight and thereby controlling ice ages.
earth-weather-0292: Which Swiss scientist became famous in the nineteenth century for demonstrating that Earth had experienced an ice age?
Louis Agassiz became known for ice age theory from 1837.
earth-weather-0293: What is the Snowball Earth hypothesis?
The snow covering mountains originally came from ancient comets
Polar ice was more extensive than today during the Jurassic
All or most of Earth's surface froze in the distant past
Earth will become a frozen ball within thousands of years
The hypothesis proposes that ice covered all or most of Earth's surface during the Proterozoic Eon.
earth-weather-0294: About 6-11 thousand years ago, the Sahara was green, with lakes and animals. What is that period called?
During the African Humid Period, the Sahara was greener because of increased monsoon rainfall.
earth-weather-0296: Which chemicals formerly used in refrigerators and aerosol sprays were found to deplete the ozone layer?
Chlorofluorocarbons release chlorine in the stratosphere, destroying ozone molecules.
earth-weather-0297: Which international agreement signed in 1987 protects the ozone layer by eliminating ozone-depleting substances?
The Montreal Protocol (1987) regulated the phaseout of ozone-depleting substances.
earth-weather-0298: Which harmful radiation does the ozone layer shield Earth from?
Visible light in its various colors
The ozone layer absorbs most harmful ultraviolet radiation coming from the Sun.
earth-weather-0300: By what Latin name is the aurora in the Northern Hemisphere known?
The northern aurora is called aurora borealis, and the southern aurora is called aurora australis.
earth-weather-0303: What is the Indian Ocean Dipole?
A river-driven salinity difference between the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea
An oscillation in the sea-surface temperature difference between the western and eastern ocean
A seasonal change in trade-wind direction over the Arabian Sea alone
A constant cold current flowing from Antarctica toward Australia's coast
The Indian Ocean Dipole is an irregular oscillation in sea-surface temperatures between the western and eastern parts of the ocean.
earth-weather-0304: What is the polar vortex in meteorology?
A large area of cold air and low pressure rotating around a pole
A sea-ice whirlpool moving slowly around Greenland
A cold ocean current circling Antarctica throughout the year
A violent tropical cyclone forming over Arctic Ocean waters
The polar vortex is a large area of low pressure and cold air surrounding the poles.
earth-weather-0306: A cool temperate climate with rain in every season
An extremely cold polar climate without a real summer
A tropical climate with distinct wet and dry seasons
A hot desert climate with rare rain throughout the year
The tropical savanna climate has a distinct dry season and a rainy season.
earth-weather-0307: What is the largest store of fresh water on Earth's surface?
About 69% of Earth's fresh water is stored in ice and glaciers.
earth-weather-0308: Which water-cycle process turns water from plant leaf surfaces into vapor?
Transpiration is the release of water vapor from plants through stomata and is part of the water cycle.
earth-weather-0309: What happens during sublimation in the water cycle?
Rainwater seeps into soil and replenishes groundwater
Ice turns directly into vapor without melting
Water vapor turns into small droplets forming clouds
Raindrops freeze in the air before reaching the ground
Sublimation is the direct transition from solid to gas, as when snow sublimates in dry mountains.
earth-weather-0310: What is drought from a climatological perspective?
A prolonged period of below-normal precipitation causing water shortage
An exceptionally low sea level at low tide that exposes coasts
An extremely hot summer day when humidity reaches its lowest levels
A season of hot, dusty winds from neighboring deserts
Drought is an extended period of deficient precipitation causing a water deficit.
earth-weather-0311: Seawater advancing over low-lying coastal land
Farmland being converted into cities and asphalt roads
Soil salinity increasing solely from irrigation with seawater
Drylands deteriorating until they lose productivity
Desertification is land degradation in arid and semiarid regions due to natural and human causes.
earth-weather-0312: Which nineteenth-century physicist demonstrated that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb heat in the atmosphere?
John Tyndall experimentally demonstrated the absorption of thermal radiation by gases such as water vapor and carbon dioxide.
earth-weather-0313: Which observatory on a Hawaiian volcano has measured atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations since 1958?
Mauna Loa Observatory has measured carbon dioxide since 1958, producing the Keeling Curve.
earth-weather-0315: What phenomenon occurs when air near the ground is colder than the air above it, trapping smoke and fog?
A temperature inversion is a warm layer above cold air that prevents pollutants from rising, causing them to accumulate near the ground.
earth-weather-0318: What is the wet-bulb temperature used to measure the danger of humid heat to humans?
The temperature at which water vapor condenses on surfaces
The lowest air temperature attainable by evaporating water into it until saturation
The highest temperature an exposed ground surface reaches in sunlight
Air temperature measured in the shade inside a Stevenson screen
Wet-bulb temperature is the lowest temperature attainable through evaporative cooling.
earth-weather-0319: Which Scottish scientist is called the 'father of modern geology' for arguing that Earth is very old and shaped by slow processes?
James Hutton is considered the father of modern geology for his ideas on deep time and slow processes.
earth-weather-0320: What is Charles Lyell's famous book published in three volumes between 1830 and 1833?
Lyell published Principles of Geology in three volumes, influencing a generation of scientists.
earth-weather-0321: Which principle states that the natural processes operating today are the same ones that shaped Earth in the past?
Uniformitarianism assumes that current natural laws and processes also operated in the past.
earth-weather-0322: Which law states that lower sedimentary layers are older than those above them unless disturbed?
The law of superposition was formulated by Nicolas Steno in the seventeenth century.
earth-weather-0323: Who drew the first geological map of an entire country, the 1815 map of England and Wales?
In 1815, William Smith published the first geological map covering an entire country.
earth-weather-0324: What is the approximate half-life of carbon-14, used to date organic remains?
Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5730 years, making it suitable for dating remains up to about 50 thousand years old.
earth-weather-0325: What is the longest division of geological time?
Geological time is divided into eons, then eras, then periods, then epochs.
earth-weather-0327: Which eon do we live in, whose name means 'visible life'?
The Phanerozoic Eon began about 539 million years ago, with an abundance of organisms with skeletons.
earth-weather-0328: During which geological era did dinosaurs dominate?
The Mesozoic Era is nicknamed the Age of Reptiles or the Age of Dinosaurs.
earth-weather-0329: What is the current geological era, which began about 66 million years ago?
The Cenozoic began after the end-Cretaceous extinction about 66 million years ago.
earth-weather-0330: What was the Cambrian explosion in the history of life?
A huge asteroid impact that suddenly ended the age of dinosaurs
An enormous volcanic eruption covering Wales in basalt during the Cambrian
The first rise in atmospheric oxygen due to cyanobacteria
The appearance of most major animal phyla in a relatively short time
The Cambrian explosion was the relatively rapid appearance of most major animal phyla in the fossil record.
earth-weather-0333: The Permian Period was named after a region in which country?
The Permian was named after the Perm region in Russia.
earth-weather-0334: Which meteorite crater in Mexico is associated with the extinction of the dinosaurs 66 million years ago?
Chicxulub Crater in Yucatan resulted from an asteroid impact associated with the end-Cretaceous extinction.
earth-weather-0335: Which element was found in unusually high concentrations in the clay layer separating the Cretaceous and Paleogene, indicating a meteorite impact?
Luis and Walter Alvarez discovered elevated iridium levels in that layer; iridium is an element common in asteroids.
earth-weather-0338: Which Canadian site is famous for preserving detailed fossils of soft-bodied animals from the Cambrian Period?
The Burgess Shale in British Columbia preserves soft-bodied Cambrian animals in exceptional detail.
earth-weather-0339: What is the current geological epoch, which began after the last ice age about 11700 years ago?
The Holocene began about 11700 years ago after the end of the last glacial period.
earth-weather-0340: Which geological epoch experienced repeated glacial cycles and was home to the woolly mammoth?
The Pleistocene was an epoch of repeated ice ages and ended about 11700 years ago.
earth-weather-0341: Which scientist discovered radioactivity, on which methods of dating rocks were later based?
Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity and received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics for it with the Curies.
earth-weather-0343: What do scientists think covered the surface of the early Earth during the Hadean Eon, when it was extremely hot?
The surface of the early Earth is thought to have been a magma ocean before it cooled and the crust formed.
earth-weather-0344: What does the term 'deep time' mean in Earth science?
The time seismic waves take to cross the entire Earth's interior
The immense span of geological time over millions and billions of years
Ocean depth measured by the time waves take to reach the bottom
The age of the deepest rocks reached by drilling to date
Deep time is the concept of geological time extending over billions of years, beyond the scales of human experience.
earth-weather-0345: What is meant by isostatic equilibrium in Earth science?
Earth rotating on its axis at a constant speed throughout the ages
All continents having the same elevation above sea level
The Moon and Sun exerting equal gravitational effects on tides
The crust floating on the mantle according to its thickness and density
Isostatic equilibrium is a state of gravitational balance in which the crust floats on the mantle according to its thickness and density.
earth-weather-0346: What has been happening to the land of Scandinavia since the melting of the ice that weighed it down during the ice age?
Scandinavia is still rising through post-glacial rebound after the weight of the ice sheets was removed.
earth-weather-0347: Which science studies ancient organisms through their fossilized remains?
Paleontology studies ancient life through fossils.
earth-weather-0348: Which English paleontologist discovered ichthyosaur skeletons on the shores of Lyme Regis in the nineteenth century?
Mary Anning became famous for her Jurassic fossil discoveries at Lyme Regis.
earth-weather-0349: Which famous meteorite crater in the Arizona desert is considered one of the best preserved?
Barringer Crater in Arizona is one of the best-preserved impact craters on Earth.
earth-weather-0351: In which desert are the Wabar meteorite craters located?
The Wabar craters are meteorite craters in the Rub al-Khali in Saudi Arabia.
earth-weather-0353: In what type of rock does oil usually accumulate after migrating from its source rock?
Impermeable salt rock through which no fluids can pass
Porous reservoir rock such as sandstone or limestone
Solid nonporous volcanic rock such as dense basalt
Crystalline metamorphic rock such as marble and quartzite
Oil migrates into porous, permeable reservoir rocks such as sandstone and carbonates, where it is trapped beneath an impermeable cap.
earth-weather-0354: What is the largest conventional oil field in the world?
Ghawar Field in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province is the largest conventional oil field in the world.
earth-weather-0355: Under which geological structure does oil often accumulate in a dome shaped like an upside-down dish?
Anticlines are among the most familiar oil traps, as oil is trapped at their crest beneath an impermeable layer.
earth-weather-0356: Which fold has rock layers that bend downward into a basin shape?
A syncline is a fold whose layers bend downward, with the youngest layers at its center.
earth-weather-0358: What is the main component of natural gas extracted from underground?
Natural gas consists mainly of methane.
earth-weather-0359: Which Muslim scholar devoted a chapter in his book Al-Shifa to mountain formation as part of his discussion of mineralogy and meteorology?
Ibn Sina's Al-Shifa contains a section on minerals and meteorology whose first chapter concerns mountain formation.
earth-weather-0360: Which Muslim scholar estimated Earth's radius with remarkable accuracy using a mountain's height and the angle of dip of the horizon?
Al-Biruni measured Earth's radius from a mountain summit by measuring the angle of dip of the horizon.
earth-weather-0361: What are the natural glass tubes or masses formed when lightning strikes sand or soil and melts it called?
Fulgurites are glass formations produced from sand or soil melted by the heat of lightning; their name comes from the Latin word for lightning.
earth-weather-0362: Which iron ore takes its name from the Greek word meaning 'blood'?
The name hematite comes from the Greek word for blood because of the red color of some varieties and its powder. It is one of the most important iron ores.
earth-weather-0363: The Volcanic Explosivity Index classifies eruption strength by the volume of erupted material. What is its highest rating?
The index runs from 0 to 8, with level 8 assigned to the greatest eruptions in geological history.
earth-weather-0364: In which atmospheric layer do noctilucent clouds, the highest clouds in Earth's atmosphere, form?
These clouds consist of ice crystals near the top of the mesosphere at an altitude of about 76?85 kilometers, above all other clouds.
earth-weather-0365: Which metamorphic rock forms when sandstone is transformed by heat and pressure?
Heat and pressure transform sandstone into quartzite, a very hard rock.
earth-weather-0366: Which opaque green mineral forms masses banded in shades of green and is a copper ore?
Malachite is an opaque, banded green copper mineral. Its color comes from copper, and it is a low-grade copper ore.
human-body-0001: What is the longest and strongest bone in the human body?
The femur is the body's longest and strongest bone and extends from the hip to the knee.
human-body-0002: What is the smallest bone in the human body, located in the middle ear?
The stapes in the middle ear is the smallest and lightest bone in the human body.
human-body-0003: How many cervical vertebrae are in the human neck?
The spine in the neck has seven cervical vertebrae, the same number as in most mammals.
human-body-0004: How many thoracic vertebrae have ribs attached to them?
There are twelve thoracic vertebrae, each articulating with a pair of ribs.
human-body-0005: How many lumbar vertebrae are usually in the human lower back?
The lumbar region has five vertebrae, which are the largest of the movable vertebrae.
human-body-0006: What is the name of the first cervical vertebra, which supports the skull?
The first vertebra is called the atlas because it supports the head as Atlas supported the sky in mythology.
human-body-0007: Around which vertebra does the first vertebra rotate when a person turns their head right and left?
The second cervical vertebra, the axis
The second cervical vertebra, the axis, has a toothlike projection around which the atlas rotates, allowing the head to turn.
human-body-0008: How many pairs of ribs are usually in the human rib cage?
The rib cage usually has twelve pairs of ribs.
human-body-0009: What are the last ribs, which do not attach to the sternum at the front, called?
The eleventh and twelfth pairs do not attach to the sternum at the front and are called floating ribs.
human-body-0010: What is the flat bone in the middle of the chest to which the ribs attach at the front?
The sternum is a long, flat bone at the front of the chest to which the upper ribs attach through cartilage.
human-body-0011: Which bone connects the shoulder to the sternum and is among the most frequently fractured bones?
The clavicle is a horizontal bone connecting the scapula and sternum and is among the most frequently fractured bones.
human-body-0012: What is the only bone in the skull that moves noticeably?
The mandible is the skull's only movable bone and articulates with the temporal bone.
human-body-0013: Which bone does not articulate with any other bone and lies in the neck above the larynx?
The hyoid bone is suspended by muscles and ligaments and does not connect directly to any other bone.
human-body-0015: To which type of bone does the patella belong, since it forms inside a muscle tendon?
The patella is a sesamoid bone that develops within the quadriceps tendon and is the largest sesamoid bone.
human-body-0016: How many bones make up the human wrist?
The wrist consists of eight small bones arranged in two rows.
human-body-0017: How many bones make up the tarsus of the foot, including the heel bone?
The tarsus consists of seven bones, the largest of which is the calcaneus, or heel bone.
human-body-0018: What is the largest bone in the foot, which forms the heel?
The calcaneus is the largest tarsal bone and forms the projection of the heel.
human-body-0019: How many phalanges are in the fingers of one hand?
Each finger has three phalanges except the thumb, which has two, making fourteen in one hand.
human-body-0020: The long bone on the inner side of the lower leg
The long bone in the arm between the shoulder and elbow
The triangular bone that forms the shoulder blade
The long bone on the thumb side of the forearm
The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm, extending from the shoulder to the elbow.
human-body-0021: Which bone is on the thumb side of the forearm?
The forearm has two bones: the radius on the thumb side and the ulna on the little-finger side.
human-body-0022: Which of the two lower-leg bones is larger and bears most of the body's weight?
The tibia, or shinbone, is the larger and stronger lower-leg bone and bears most of the weight.
human-body-0023: What is the triangular bone at the base of the spine that consists of five fused vertebrae called?
The sacrum is a triangular bone formed by the fusion of five vertebrae and lies between the hip bones.
human-body-0024: Which cells build new bone tissue?
Osteoblasts secrete bone material and build new bone.
human-body-0025: Which large, multinucleated cells break down bone tissue so it can be remodeled?
Osteoclasts dissolve bone tissue as part of its continuous renewal.
human-body-0026: Which fibrous membrane covers the outside of bones except at joint surfaces?
The periosteum is a membrane covering the outer surface of bone; it is absent from joint surfaces.
human-body-0027: Which mineral do bones store in large quantities, giving them their hardness?
Bones store most of the body's calcium in the form of calcium phosphate salts.
human-body-0028: Which type of marrow fills the cavities of long bones in adults and consists mainly of fat?
Yellow marrow consists mainly of fat cells and fills the shafts of long bones in adults.
human-body-0030: Why is a baby born with more bones than an adult has?
Because the baby's bones fall out and are replaced
Because the extra bones turn into cartilage
Because some bones fuse during growth
Because some bones dissolve after birth
A child is born with about 270 bones, some of which fuse during growth to become 206 in adulthood.
human-body-0031: What type of joint is the shoulder joint?
The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint: the rounded head of the humerus sits within the scapula's socket, allowing movement in many directions.
human-body-0032: What type of joint is the elbow, which moves in one direction like a door?
The elbow is a hinge joint that permits bending and straightening in one plane, like a door hinge.
human-body-0034: What fluid fills the cavities of movable joints and reduces friction between the ends of bones?
Synovial fluid lubricates joints and reduces friction between the articular cartilages.
human-body-0035: Which fibrous tissue connects one bone to another at a joint?
A ligament is fibrous connective tissue joining bones to one another, whereas a tendon joins muscle to bone.
human-body-0036: Which smooth, flexible tissue covers the ends of bones at joints and forms the outer ear?
Cartilage is flexible connective tissue that covers joint surfaces and forms the framework of the outer ear and the tip of the nose.
human-body-0037: Why does injured cartilage heal very slowly compared with bone?
Because it has no blood vessels
Because it is subjected to greater pressure than bone
Because it is always immersed in synovial fluid
Because it contains no living cells
Cartilage has no blood vessels, so nutrients reach it by slow diffusion and its renewal is slow.
human-body-0038: What are the fibrocartilage cushions that separate the vertebrae and absorb shocks?
Intervertebral discs are fibrocartilaginous structures that act as shock-absorbing cushions and allow the spine to move.
human-body-0039: In which disease does bone density decrease, making bones fragile and easily broken?
Osteoporosis is a loss of bone mass and deterioration of its structure, increasing the risk of fractures.
human-body-0040: A deficiency of which vitamin causes rickets and soft bones in children?
Rickets most often results from a deficiency of vitamin D, which is necessary for calcium absorption.
human-body-0041: What is the broad end of a long bone that contains spongy bone called?
The epiphysis is the broad end of a long bone, while the diaphysis is its central shaft.
human-body-0043: How many bones usually make up the skull, including its cranial and facial parts?
The human skull usually consists of 22 bones, excluding the ear ossicles.
human-body-0044: What are the immovable fibrous joints connecting the cranial bones called?
The cranial bones are joined by interlocking fibrous joints called sutures, which are almost immovable.
human-body-0045: Which bone forms the back and base of the skull and contains the large opening for the spinal cord?
The occipital bone is at the back of the skull and contains the foramen magnum, through which the spinal cord passes.
human-body-0046: What is the flat, triangular bone in the upper back known as the shoulder blade?
The scapula is a flat, triangular bone connecting the humerus to the clavicle.
human-body-0047: What is the largest bone in the pelvis, whose upper edge can be felt at the waist?
The ilium is the largest and uppermost part of the hip bone; its upper edge is the iliac crest.
human-body-0048: Which two crossing ligaments inside the knee joint prevent the lower leg from sliding forward and backward?
The anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments cross in an X shape inside the knee and stabilize it.
human-body-0049: What are the two menisci in the knee joint?
Two cartilage pads that absorb shocks between the thigh and lower leg
Two small bones supporting the patella on either side
Two strong ligaments connecting the patella to the shinbone
Two fluid-filled sacs preventing friction between tendon and skin
A meniscus is a crescent-shaped piece of cartilage that distributes the load and absorbs shocks in the knee.
human-body-0050: Which facial bone forms the prominence of the cheek below the eye?
The zygomatic bone forms the prominence of the cheek and the lateral wall of the eye socket.
human-body-0052: What is the longest muscle in the human body, running diagonally across the front of the thigh?
The sartorius is the longest muscle in the body and extends from the hip to the inner side of the knee.
human-body-0053: What is the smallest skeletal muscle in the human body?
The stapedius, which stabilizes the stapes bone, is the smallest skeletal muscle in the body.
human-body-0055: What are the three types of muscle tissue in the human body?
There are three muscle types: voluntary skeletal muscle, smooth muscle in the walls of internal organs, and cardiac muscle in the heart.
human-body-0056: Which type of muscle lines the walls of the stomach, intestines, and blood vessels?
Smooth muscles are involuntary and occur in the walls of hollow organs such as the stomach and blood vessels.
human-body-0057: What are the two main proteins that slide past one another to produce muscle contraction?
According to the sliding filament theory, actin filaments slide past myosin filaments, shortening the muscle fiber.
human-body-0058: When the biceps contracts to bend the elbow, which muscle on the opposite side relaxes?
The biceps and triceps are antagonistic muscles: the first bends the elbow and the second straightens it.
human-body-0059: Which triangular muscle covers the shoulder joint and gives it its rounded shape?
The deltoid is a triangular muscle covering the shoulder and is responsible for raising the arm sideways.
human-body-0060: What is the strongest and thickest tendon in the human body, connecting the calf muscle to the heel bone?
The Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the calcaneus and is the body's strongest and thickest tendon.
human-body-0061: Which substance was formerly believed to cause muscle pain after exertion and is produced when oxygen is scarce?
Lactic acid was formerly believed to cause muscle pain, but lactate is actually a metabolic product that does not cause delayed soreness.
human-body-0062: What protein pigment stores oxygen inside muscle cells?
Myoglobin is a muscle protein that stores oxygen and gives meat its red color.
human-body-0063: What is the condition in which muscles stiffen several hours after death?
Rigor mortis is muscle stiffening after death due to depletion of ATP, which is needed for muscle relaxation.
human-body-0064: How many chambers does the human heart have?
The heart has four chambers: two atria above and two ventricles below.
human-body-0065: Which heart chamber has the thickest wall because it pumps blood throughout the body?
The left ventricle pumps blood throughout the body through the aorta, so its wall is thicker than that of the right ventricle.
human-body-0066: What is the valve between the left atrium and left ventricle called?
The mitral, or bicuspid, valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle.
human-body-0067: What is the valve between the right atrium and right ventricle called?
The tricuspid valve has three leaflets and lies between the right atrium and right ventricle.
human-body-0068: What produces the two heart sounds heard through a stethoscope, 'lub-dub'?
Expansion of the lungs against the heart wall
The first sound comes from the closing of the two atrioventricular valves and the second from the closing of the two semilunar valves.
human-body-0069: What area in the wall of the right atrium initiates the heartbeat and is called the natural pacemaker?
The sinoatrial node generates the electrical impulses that set the heart's rhythm.
human-body-0070: What is the two-layered membrane that surrounds and protects the heart?
The pericardium is a fibroserous sac enclosing the heart and the roots of the major blood vessels.
human-body-0071: Which arteries supply the heart muscle itself with blood?
The coronary arteries branch from the root of the aorta and supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood.
human-body-0072: What is the largest artery in the human body?
The aorta leaves the left ventricle and branches to supply the whole body; it is the largest artery.
human-body-0073: Which blood vessel carries oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs?
The pulmonary artery is an exception among arteries: it carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
human-body-0074: Which vessels return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the heart?
The pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
human-body-0075: Which of the two large veins returns blood from the legs and abdomen to the right atrium?
The inferior vena cava collects blood from the lower half of the body and empties it into the right atrium.
human-body-0076: What are the smallest blood vessels, through whose walls gases and nutrients are exchanged with cells?
Capillary walls are one cell layer thick, allowing substances to pass through easily.
human-body-0077: What prevents blood from flowing backward in the veins of the legs?
High blood pressure in the veins
Veins contain valves that permit blood to flow only toward the heart and prevent backflow.
human-body-0078: Which English scientist described in the seventeenth century how the heart pumps blood around the whole body?
In 1628, William Harvey published his book demonstrating systemic circulation driven by the heart's pumping.
human-body-0079: What is the normal resting heart rate for an adult?
An adult's normal resting pulse usually ranges from 60 to 100 beats per minute.
human-body-0080: What unit is usually used to measure blood pressure?
Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury because mercury gauges were historically used.
human-body-0081: What does the higher number in a blood pressure reading such as 120/80 represent?
Diastolic pressure when the heart relaxes
The number of heartbeats per minute
The percentage of oxygen in the blood
Systolic pressure when the heart contracts
The higher number is systolic pressure and the lower number is diastolic pressure between beats.
human-body-0082: Approximately how many liters of blood are in an adult human body?
An adult's blood volume is about five liters, or around 7% of body weight.
human-body-0083: What is the yellowish liquid part of blood that makes up more than half its volume?
Plasma is a pale yellow liquid constituting about 55% of blood volume; it carries cells and dissolved substances.
human-body-0084: How long does a red blood cell live on average before being replaced?
A red blood cell lives for about 100 to 120 days before being removed in the spleen and liver.
human-body-0085: What distinguishes mature human red blood cells from most other body cells?
They are the largest blood cells
Mature red blood cells in mammals lose their nuclei to make room for more hemoglobin.
human-body-0086: What shape is a human red blood cell?
A red blood cell is a disc concave on both sides, increasing its surface area for gas exchange.
human-body-0087: Which metallic element in hemoglobin binds oxygen?
Hemoglobin contains iron in the heme group, where oxygen binds.
human-body-0088: Which Austrian scientist discovered blood groups in 1901?
Karl Landsteiner discovered blood groups A, B, and O and received a Nobel Prize for the discovery.
human-body-0089: Which blood group is known as the universal donor for red blood cells?
O negative red blood cells have no A, B, or D antigens, making them suitable for most patients.
human-body-0090: Which blood group is known as the universal recipient because it can receive red blood cells from all blood groups?
AB positive blood contains no antibodies against A, B, or D antigens.
human-body-0091: Which protein dissolved in plasma turns into fibrin strands when blood clots?
Thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin strands that form the clot's mesh.
human-body-0092: Which vitamin is necessary for the formation of blood-clotting factors in the liver?
Vitamin K is necessary for the formation of several clotting factors, and its deficiency causes easy bleeding.
human-body-0093: What inherited disease delays blood clotting because of a deficiency of a clotting factor?
Hemophilia is an inherited disorder involving a deficiency of clotting factor VIII or IX, which prolongs bleeding.
human-body-0095: Which hormone do the kidneys secrete to stimulate bone marrow to produce red blood cells?
The kidney secretes erythropoietin when oxygen is low, increasing red blood cell production.
human-body-0096: Which artery is usually felt for a pulse at the wrist on the thumb side?
The pulse is commonly felt over the radial artery at the wrist on the thumb side.
human-body-0097: Which two arteries on either side of the neck supply the head and brain with blood?
The right and left carotid arteries ascend the neck to supply the head and brain.
human-body-0098: Which vessel carries nutrient-rich blood from the intestines to the liver before it reaches the heart?
The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestines and spleen to the liver for processing.
human-body-0099: Which heart chamber receives blood returning from the body through the two venae cavae?
The superior and inferior venae cavae empty deoxygenated blood into the right atrium.
human-body-0101: What are the tiny air sacs in the lungs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged?
Alveoli are surrounded by capillaries, and gases are exchanged across their thin walls.
human-body-0102: How many lobes does the human right lung have?
The right lung has three lobes, while the left has two to leave room for the heart.
human-body-0103: Why is the left lung slightly smaller than the right lung?
Because the stomach lies directly above it
Because the liver presses on it from below
Because the trachea tilts toward it
To leave room for the heart
The heart tilts to the left, so the left lung leaves a recess for it called the cardiac notch.
human-body-0104: What shape are the cartilage rings supporting the wall of the trachea and keeping it open?
The trachea is supported by C-shaped cartilage rings that are incomplete at the back.
human-body-0105: Where in the human body are the vocal cords located?
The vocal cords are two folds inside the larynx that vibrate as air passes, producing sound.
human-body-0106: What is the visible cartilage prominence at the front of the neck that is more pronounced in men?
The first cartilage ring of the trachea
The Adam's apple is the prominence of the thyroid cartilage in the larynx and enlarges in males after puberty.
human-body-0107: What double membrane covers each lung and lines the chest wall?
The pleura has two layers with fluid between them that helps the lung slide during breathing.
human-body-0109: Which part of the brain controls involuntary breathing?
Respiratory centers in the medulla oblongata and pons of the brainstem automatically regulate the breathing rhythm.
human-body-0110: An increased blood concentration of which gas stimulates the respiratory center to increase the breathing rate?
An increase in blood carbon dioxide is the strongest stimulus for increasing the breathing rate.
human-body-0112: Spasms in the stomach muscles after eating
A sudden involuntary contraction of the diaphragm
A temporary blockage in the nose
Hiccups are repeated involuntary contractions of the diaphragm followed by closure of the vocal cords, producing the sound.
human-body-0114: Approximately what percentage of exhaled air is oxygen?
Inhaled air contains about 21% oxygen, and about 14 to 16% remains in exhaled air.
human-body-0115: Which enzyme in saliva begins starch digestion in the mouth?
Salivary amylase begins breaking starch down into simpler sugars during chewing.
human-body-0116: What wave-like muscular movement propels food through the esophagus and intestines?
Peristalsis consists of successive smooth-muscle contractions that propel food through the digestive tract.
human-body-0117: What strong acid does the stomach secrete to help digestion and kill germs?
Parietal cells in the stomach secrete hydrochloric acid, making its environment highly acidic.
human-body-0118: What is the main stomach enzyme that begins protein digestion?
Pepsin is a stomach enzyme that breaks down proteins and is active in an acidic environment.
human-body-0120: What is the partially digested food passing from the stomach into the intestines called?
Chyme is a semifluid mass of partially digested food that passes from the stomach into the duodenum.
human-body-0121: Which ring-shaped muscle controls food leaving the stomach for the intestines?
The pyloric sphincter at the stomach's outlet regulates the passage of chyme into the duodenum.
human-body-0122: What is the first part of the small intestine after the stomach?
The small intestine has three parts: the duodenum, then the jejunum, then the ileum.
human-body-0123: What are the tiny fingerlike projections in the small intestine's lining that increase the absorption area?
Villi greatly increase the surface area of the small intestine, facilitating nutrient absorption.
human-body-0125: What is the main function of the large intestine?
Absorbing water and salts from food remains
The large intestine absorbs water and salts from food remains before they are expelled.
human-body-0126: A part of the stomach near the esophagus
A small blind-ended tube attached to the cecum
A small gland above the kidney
The appendix is a narrow, closed-ended tube branching from the cecum at the start of the large intestine.
human-body-0127: What is the largest gland and largest internal organ in the human body?
The liver is the body's largest gland and lies in the upper right side of the abdomen.
human-body-0128: Which organ can rebuild itself even if a large part of it is removed?
The liver has a unique ability to regenerate, growing back after a large part has been removed.
human-body-0129: What is the digestive function of the bile secreted by the liver?
Turning fats into small droplets that are easy to digest
Bile emulsifies fats, breaking them into droplets that lipase can digest easily.
human-body-0130: Which organ secretes digestive enzymes into the intestine and also secretes insulin into the blood?
The pancreas is a dual-function gland: it secretes digestive juice into the duodenum and insulin and glucagon into the blood.
human-body-0131: Which pigment is produced by hemoglobin breakdown and gives bile its color?
Bilirubin results from the breakdown of heme in old blood cells and is excreted in bile.
human-body-0132: What is the yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes caused by elevated blood bilirubin called?
Jaundice is yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes due to bilirubin accumulation.
human-body-0133: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
The enamel covering a tooth's crown is the hardest substance in the human body.
human-body-0134: What tissue lies beneath tooth enamel and makes up most of the tooth's mass?
Dentin is a calcified tissue forming most of the tooth and is covered by enamel at the crown.
human-body-0135: How many primary teeth does a child have?
A child has twenty primary teeth, which fall out and are replaced by permanent teeth.
human-body-0136: Which molars appear at the back of the mouth relatively late, usually between the ages of 17 and 25?
Wisdom teeth are the third molars and usually erupt between the ages of 17 and 25.
human-body-0137: Which pointed teeth are used to tear food, with two in each jaw?
Canines are pointed teeth with long roots that tear food; each jaw has two.
human-body-0138: Which sharp front teeth cut food?
Incisors are front teeth with flat cutting edges that cut food when biting.
human-body-0140: What is the largest human salivary gland, located in front of the ear?
The parotid is the largest salivary gland and lies in front of and below the ear.
human-body-0141: Approximately how many liters of saliva does an adult produce daily?
About a quarter of a liter
An adult produces approximately 0.75 to 1.5 liters of saliva daily.
human-body-0142: Which microorganisms live in the large intestine and produce some vitamins, such as vitamin K?
Beneficial intestinal bacteria aid digestion and produce vitamins, including vitamin K.
human-body-0143: Which enzyme digests milk sugar, with its deficiency causing lactose intolerance?
Lactase breaks lactose down into glucose and galactose; its deficiency causes disturbances after drinking milk.
human-body-0144: Which fat-digesting enzyme is secreted by the pancreas?
Pancreatic lipase breaks triglycerides down into free fatty acids and monoglycerides.
human-body-0145: What muscular tube carries food from the pharynx to the stomach?
The esophagus is a muscular tube extending behind the trachea and carrying food to the stomach.
human-body-0146: Approximately how long is an adult human esophagus?
An adult's esophagus is about 25 centimeters long.
human-body-0147: What large serous membrane lines the abdominal wall and covers most abdominal organs?
The peritoneum is a serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering most of its internal organs.
human-body-0148: In what form does the liver store excess glucose for release when needed?
The liver stores excess glucose as glycogen and converts it back into glucose when blood sugar falls.
human-body-0149: Which toxic substance does the liver convert into less harmful urea?
The liver converts ammonia produced by protein breakdown into urea through the urea cycle.
human-body-0150: What is the largest part of the human brain?
The cerebrum, with its two hemispheres, is the largest part of the brain and is responsible for thought, perception, and voluntary movement.
human-body-0151: What broad bundle of nerve fibers connects the right and left cerebral hemispheres?
The corpus callosum is a large bundle of nerve fibers connecting the cerebral hemispheres and transmitting information between them.
human-body-0152: Which brain lobe is primarily responsible for processing vision?
The primary visual cortex lies in the occipital lobe at the back of the brain.
human-body-0153: In which brain lobe is the primary auditory cortex located?
The auditory cortex is in the temporal lobe on the side of the brain near the ear.
human-body-0154: Which brain lobe is most closely associated with planning, decision-making, and behavioral control?
The frontal lobe, particularly its prefrontal cortex, is responsible for executive functions such as planning and behavioral control.
human-body-0155: Which brain area, named after a French physician, is associated with speech production?
Broca's area lies in the frontal lobe; damage to it impairs speech production while comprehension often remains intact.
human-body-0156: Which brain structure resembles a seahorse and plays an important role in forming new memories?
The hippocampus is named for its resemblance to a seahorse and is essential for memory consolidation.
human-body-0158: Which part of the brain regulates body temperature and the sensations of hunger and thirst?
The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis: temperature, hunger, thirst, and pituitary hormone secretion.
human-body-0159: If the left cerebral hemisphere is injured, movement on which side of the body is most likely to be affected?
Each cerebral hemisphere controls movement on the opposite side of the body because the nerve pathways cross.
human-body-0160: Approximately what is the average mass of an adult human brain?
An adult brain weighs about 1.2 to 1.4 kilograms, approximately 2% of body weight.
human-body-0161: Approximately what percentage of the body's energy does the brain consume at rest?
The brain consumes about 20% of the body's energy although it accounts for only about 2% of body weight.
human-body-0162: Approximately how many nerve cells are in the human brain?
Studies estimate that the human brain contains about 86 billion neurons.
human-body-0163: What are the three membranes that surround and protect the brain and spinal cord?
The meninges are three membranes: the dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater.
human-body-0165: What long extension of a nerve cell carries signals away from the cell body?
The axon carries impulses from the cell body to other cells.
human-body-0166: What short branches of a nerve cell receive signals from other cells?
Dendrites receive signals and convey them to the cell body.
human-body-0167: What fatty covering surrounds many axons and speeds up signal transmission?
The myelin sheath is a fatty insulator that makes the signal jump between nodes of Ranvier, allowing faster transmission.
human-body-0168: What is the junction between two nerve cells where a signal is transmitted called?
A synapse is the junction of a neuron with another cell, where signals are usually transmitted by chemical messengers.
